title: Could Meta fix its glasses privacy issues with an LED redesign?
snippet: The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone? more…
fullText:
The smart glasses race is heating up as Meta and Samsung are about to go head-to-head, but could a new Meta glasses style fix the privacy stigma, or are things too far gone?

Meta launched its own-branded smart glasses this summer (read: with no Ray-Ban or Oakley branding), and they seem to have done well for a number of reasons. Some models are much cheaper than Ray-Ban-branded pairs, while other Meta glasses carry Kylie Jenner or LISA names, bringing in a unique note of fashion, but none of these models changed the look of the camera LED indicator on the front.

😎The Meta Glasses Black Friday sale has begun!

Meta has come under fire over the past two years as people have abused the company’s smart glasses, giving them the unfortunate term “perv glasses” on social media because some people disabled the camera LED, which is supposed to illuminate when the camera is recording. Meta has issued several different software patches to disable the glasses’ camera when the LED is tampered with, but many have begun to feel like having a camera on smart glasses just feels wrong after people have abused the technology.

Meta glasses product lead David Woodland posted a render of the Gentle Monster cateye style glasses in a now-deleted Tweet on X on November 17, simply saying “I plead the fifth.” Presumably, he was calling out how similar these glasses look to the Meta Starfire Kylie Jenner style, but we’ll likely never know now.

	

Samsung and Google’s Warby Parker and Gentle Monster glasses certainly resemble Meta’s glasses, but they also do something noticeably different: the camera LED doesn’t look like the camera on the other side.

So this begs the question: can Meta do anything to salvage the unsavory association its glasses now have attached to them? We covered this topic on episode 125 of our Pixelated podcast, and Woodland’s post further highlights the question. A camera LED that’s obviously different from the camera on the other side would likely prompt people to ask about your glasses, while Meta’s design is purposefully stealthy because of its symmetry.

Does this design difference help Samsung’s Gentle Monster/Warby Parker glasses feel more private, and would a similar redesign help Meta’s glasses? I think it would help a lot, but I also want to know what our readers think. What say you, folks?

title: Major privacy breaches reported in Muse AI – company responds [U]
snippet: Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse, currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads. This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user … more…
fullText:
Meta employees have expressed concerns about what appear to be major privacy breaches when using Muse, currently the second most popular free iPhone app in the App Store with over 10 million downloads.

This includes again accessing end-to-end encrypted messaging without permission, and sharing what may be the bank balances of another Muse user …

Siri AI was not the only AI app to launch back in September; Meta’s Muse AI app was launched the same month, with the company describing it as “your personal AI agent that gets things done across every part of life.”

Muse initially launched as an iPhone app, with Mac and iPad apps following shortly afterwards. It immediately moved to the top of the US App Store charts, overtaking ChatGPT. It quickly exceeded 5 million downloads following a major advertising push by Meta, and that number has since doubled.

Privacy concerns quickly raised

It wasn’t long before major privacy concerns were raised. Tech writer Jason Aten reported that the Mac app accessed his messages despite him explicitly refusing permission. The app then lied to him about how it had achieved this. Meta described this as a bug.

Security researcher Patrick Wardle also discovered a zero-day vulnerability that could allow an attacker to hijack dictated prompts, directing them instead to their own server.

I said at the time that I would absolutely not be one of the millions of people using the app, and the wisdom of that decision has now been underlined by a fresh report.

Reuters now reports Meta employees discussing further breaches. This includes another example of accessing encrypted messages without permission.

An employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

The report says this appears to have been done by capturing push notifications. However, this was what the app claimed had happened in the earlier case, and it turned out not to be true. The AI Now Institute was able to replicate the problem of Muse accessing Signal messages without permission.

Another employee reported receiving unsolicited bank balances that they say appeared to be those of another Muse user. 

Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

Meta told Reuters that these were “isolated incidents” and suggested that the bank balances may have been AI hallucinations rather than leaked information. Update: Meta has now told us that the balances were definitely hallucinations.

	

Meta has taken issue with the messaging claims. It says that access to either notifications or messaging must be explicitly granted.

With Android, users have the option to grant apps notification access, which allows apps to see notifications as they’re received. This is something users need to opt in to and is not specific to Muse. With Mac, to allow Muse to work on your behalf, you not only need to click allow for accessibility and screen recording, but after that it takes you to a settings screen where you once again need to confirm and turn this on.

The company also implies that the experience of employees may relate to internal versions of Muse.

Employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.

9to5Mac’s Take

I can only repeat my previous take on Muse: Nope.

title: These tech outages are giving Y2K, AI agent style
snippet: Are the recent outages in the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms really a coincidence? There's actually likely something deeper going on, cybersecurity experts say.
fullText:
It’s going down, as the American rapper Yung Joc might say: the airline booking systems, banking platforms, and productivity platforms. In the past two weeks, the U.S.’s top businesses have faced technical outages that have disrupted the systems that run everyday life.  

Apple Pay went down. NASA’s internal communication network went down. The FAA had to ground all flights for hours (only the third time in history since 9/11), and Microsoft was hit with an outage that took down Outlook, Teams, and Copilot for nearly two days.

The first thought, naturally, is an AI hacker invasion of some sort, especially after hackers managed to attack fridges in a grocery store and a blood bank in France a few weeks ago. Here in the U.S., the director of National Intelligence said these outages don’t seem related to state-sponsored terrorism, while President Trump called the issues “individual events.” Many of the companies themselves have said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks or AI attacks, but tech issues.

Only, there’s the fact that they all struck within a short timespan of each other, and just a few weeks after Cybersecurity’s so-called “Black October,” when a slew of also-unrelated cybersecurity incidents occurred on October 21, striking PHP, Node.js, LiteLLM, more.

While there’s no reason to view these outages as cyberattacks, there may be more than coincidence going on: It’s giving AI-native Y2K, frankly. 

Dave DeWalt, an investor who worked in cybersecurity for more than three decades (including as president and CEO of McAfee and as vice chairman of the CISA Advisory Council for the Department of Homeland Security), also thinks it’s probably AI-related.

The technical outages are most likely the “growing pains of a security system that’s getting stronger, not weaker,” and that “AI is surfacing vulnerabilities at a speed and scale we’ve never had before through AI tools like Mythos and others,” he told TechCrunch.

The thing is, many of these technical flaws have always existed, but because AI is surfacing them so fast, enterprises are rushing to fix them before bad actors can exploit them. “That surge in patching is disrupting things in the short term,” he said.

This was, perhaps, the first moment when legacy meets modern, Anusha Iyer, a software engineer and founder of the security startup Corsha, told TechCrunch. “These industrial systems were never designed to be connected, let alone securely connected in the way we are pushing them to be today,” she said. 

Virginia Senator Mark Warner, vice chair of the Senate Intel Committee, came to a similar conclusion (although investigations are still underway as to what could be happening). “These disruptions should serve as a wake-up call. It feels like every day brings another reminder that AI is moving faster than our ability to manage its consequences,” the senator wrote on X. 

AI is reshaping how software is built, deployed, and operated, on a scale where everyone feels the sharp learning curve. Iyer cited the FAA outage as an example of legacy tech that is not as sophisticated or advanced as the technologies companies are trying to merge it with. 

In less technical terms, she said the outage may have been caused (and preliminary findings point to this) when the FAA was trying to modernize its telecommunications infrastructure and the transition overwhelmed parts of its legacy hardware, where the new tech likely operated at a normal modern capacity while the legacy hardware couldn’t keep up. 

When looked at this way, she said, AI is actually getting the bad rep. “It’s not rapid adoption of AI yet causing these outages,” she said. “The fault is the rushed mix of the legacy and modern systems without a clear understanding of operational and cyber risk or the ability to gatekeep and protect the legacy systems.” 

Organizations need a more steadfast approach to AI adoption, including more testing and prioritizing what needs to be fixed and when, DeWalt said. 

Iyer added, “These industrial systems need to be segmented more tightly and more access controlled, so as modern systems are introduced, it can be phased in and risk mitigated.” 

Actually, there might be a silver lining to all of this for companies (and for venture investors). DeWalt said he’d rather see these U.S. enterprises find and patch their flaws, even in this messy way, than have bad actors find and exploit those vulnerabilities in AI warfare that could cause even more national security issues. 

And maybe some aspiring founders were inspired by them. DeWalt expects a rise in companies focused on “AI-driven vulnerability management, autonomous remediation, safe patch testing and deployment, and resilience for the systems that keep critical infrastructure running,” he said.

“There’s real pain in this transition as we’ve seen in the past week,” DeWalt said. “But there’s also enormous opportunity for the companies that help organizations move at AI speed without breaking things.”

title: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
snippet: In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn't belong to them.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

9:38 AM PST · November 19, 2026

Image Credits:Meta

		

							

											
									

					

	

Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts. 

In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them. 

One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app. 

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.

“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.” 

Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.

title: The Xiaomi 18 Pro debuts globally with sub-mm bezels, privacy display, rear display, and 200MP Leica cameras
snippet: Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC. more…
fullText:
Xiaomi is pushing the limits of modern smartphone specs with a killer design, flush camera lenses, and a next-gen Snapdragon SoC.

If you’re looking for a phone with top-tier specs, Xiaomi has a new phone for you. The Xiaomi 18 Pro and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max are the company’s latest flagships, available starting today, November 17. When looking at the spec list for the Xiaomi 18 series, it’s difficult to find anything that was left out.

During the launch presentation, Xiaomi emphasized that its new privacy display wasn’t just a copy of “other privacy displays.” Rather, they created an entirely new subpixel layout called HyperRGB 2.0 that delivers far higher resolution and brightness output than the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. You can also enable and disable the privacy display feature on the Xiaomi 18 Pro series with a click of the new AI button on the left side of the phone. Functionally, Xiaomi’s privacy display looks nearly identical to Samsung’s, including the ability to have specific apps use it.

Both models feature identical specs, including the privacy display and cameras, with the exception of the screen size, battery capacity, and charging speed. Here are the differences:

	

Spec

Xiaomi 18 Pro

Xiaomi 18 Pro Max

Display size

6.4-inches

6.9-inches

Battery capacity

6,000mAh

7,050mAh

Charging speed

90W wired, 50W wireless

100W wired, 50W wireless

The 120Hz LTPO display is bordered by a 0.99mm bezel, the smallest in the industry so far, 4,000-nit peak brightness, and TÜV Rheinland Triple Eye Care Certification, including a 2160Hz PWM dimming rate. Inside the phone is a Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 processor with a 3D IceLoop cooling system, and each model’s silicon-carbon battery includes 28% silicon content.

On the back is a pair of 200MP cameras, including a 1/1.28-inch main sensor and a 1/1.56-inch periscope telephoto sensor. These are massive sensors, especially compared to the 1/3.94″ and 1/2.52″ telephoto sensors in the Galaxy S26 Ultra. Despite their size, Xiaomi packs them onto the back in an island with fully flat glass — no protruding camera lenses!

That island on the back isn’t just for cameras, though. It also packs in a 120Hz LTPO M11 OLED panel with 4,000-nit peak brightness for ultra-high-quality selfies and group shots, plus support for notifications and apps. Xiaomi created a new GenAI Apps feature that lets you create your own apps on the back display, plus official support for several popular apps like Google Maps, Spotify, and more.

The Xiaomi 18 Pro series ships with HyperOS 4 (Android 17) and includes 3 months of Google AI Pro, plus 5TB of Google Cloud storage. The Xiaomi 18 Pro retails for €1399 for the model with 12GB RAM and 256GB storage, or €1599 for 12GB/512GB. The Xiaomi 18 Pro Max starts at €1599 for 12GB/256GB, €1799 for 12GB/512GB, and a 16GB/1TB model will be available soon for €2099.

Some retailers also sell a bundle that includes the Official silicone magnetic case, which usually retails for €39, as well as the Magnetic Remote Stand, which retails for €69. That remote stand functions as a MagSafe-style stand and remote, giving you camera shutter functionality and a scrolling feature.

title: tvOS 27.3 beta 2 brings Siri AI to Apple TV beta testers
snippet: Following the rollout of Siri AI to select Apple TV models with tvOS 27.2.1, Apple today expanded availability to users running the tvOS 27.3 developer beta. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following the rollout of Siri AI to select Apple TV models with tvOS 27.2.1, Apple today expanded availability to users running the tvOS 27.3 developer beta. Here are the details.

Siri AI arrives for tvOS beta testers on select models

Last Friday, Apple released tvOS 27.2.1, bringing the new Siri AI to Apple TV 4K 2nd-gen and 3rd-gen models. The feature requires a nearby, paired device with Siri AI enabled.

The update came just hours after the official launch of the Apple TV 4K (4th generation), which ships with Siri AI support out of the box.

However, users running tvOS 27.3 beta 1 still had no access to the new Siri AI. This means that although the feature was available in the latest public release, users on the beta were left without it.

Earlier tonight, Apple released tvOS 27.3 beta 2, which, as leaker pdfu noted in a post on X, now includes a new setup screen inviting users to enable Siri AI.

9to5Mac was able to confirm the change, with the new splash screen introducing Siri AI and giving users the option to try the new assistant or continue using Siri Classic.

With Siri AI now available on both the public and beta versions of tvOS, the new HomePod mini 2 is still waiting for the feature. Apple previously confirmed that Siri AI would arrive in a future software update, but it was not included in last Friday’s HomePod 27.2.1 release, and the company has yet to announce a rollout date.

title: Signal now blocks screenshots on iPhone to stop Siri AI from seeing chats
snippet: Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Popular secure messaging app Signal has rolled out a new update that automatically disables screenshots for the sake of blocking Siri AI from reading your chats. Here are the details.

Signal update disables iPhone screenshots by default as a new privacy protection

Signal’s latest app update on iPhone disables a key system feature: taking screenshots.

As Signal told Reuters, that’s because Apple doesn’t currently provide better tools for iOS developers to safeguard app content from Siri AI and third-party AI agents.

By default, users who update and try to take a screenshot will see a message that says: “Screenshot prevented by ‘Block Siri AI’ setting.” 

Fortunately, there’s an easy workaround. Users who want to re-enable screenshots can do so by visiting Signal’s privacy settings and turning off the new toggle that’s labeled ‘Block Siri AI.’

Here’s 9to5Mac’s own Arin Waichulis:

Signal now blocks in-app screenshots on iPhone to keep Siri AI from reading chats

It’s a new toggle in settings that’s on by default, but can be turned off

No equivalent for its Mac app pic.twitter.com/ImsinqMNPq

— Arin (@arinwaichulis) November 20, 2026

Here’s exactly what that toggle does, per the in-app settings:

Prevent Siri AI from scanning Signal content. This will also block you from taking screenshots in the app and App Switcher.

It’s good to see that users can manually disable the new privacy setting if they want. But Signal’s decision to block screenshots does raise important questions about the potential gap in privacy tools for iOS developers.

Apple already lets you block Siri AI from accessing whichever apps you manually exclude, and that became even easier in iOS 27.2. But rather than directing users to that system option, Signal seems to believe it needed to take action itself with this update.

title: Apple may be developing its own AI agent that runs your Mac
snippet: The iPhone maker appears to be building agents that can compete with the likes of Meta Muse, Instinct, Claude, and OpenAI Dots.
fullText:
Apple appears to be working on its own AI agent to conduct computer work on behalf of users — including using apps, accessing websites, and coding, among other things.

The news was originally reported by Bloomberg, which spotted a job listing the iPhone maker recently posted for a senior engineering manager to oversee the creation of an “AI agent that can use a computer.”

“Imagine an AI agent that can use a computer the way a capable person does,” the posting says. “It browses the web, works across apps, runs commands, writes and debugs code, and calls services, and it chooses the right tool for each step. It does all this privately and with the polish people expect from Apple.” 

The posting additionally notes that the agents should be able to move “fluidly between tools” and “carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs.”

TechCrunch reached out to Apple for more information but did not receive a response. 

Agents capable of computer work have become one of the hottest commodities in the tech industry over the past year. Major labs like Anthropic and OpenAI have launched such services, while other major tech brands — like Meta, which recently launched its Muse agent line — have also moved into the space. It makes sense that Apple — which is trying to expand its AI offerings in the new John Ternus era — would want to follow suit.

Bloomberg additionally notes that, at the same time that Apple is working on its own digital assistant, the company is making it significantly harder for third-party agents to gain total control over its computers. 

The outlet notes that the version of its upcoming macOS 27.3 will deploy warnings discouraging users from granting full access to third-party agents. In October, Apple issued a notification to developers stating that the company planned to “introduce additional controls to ensure that users who genuinely wish to grant an app this extraordinary level of access can only do so with very explicit user action.”

Bloomberg writes that while the iPhone maker “has eyed introducing the service as soon as the end of next year,” progress on its in-house agent “remains in the early stages.”

title: Anthropic rival says companies can (mostly) skip the pricey models
snippet: On the day Anthropic went public, Fireworks AI’s co-founder made the case for open source models as a cheaper alternative, and addressed the breaches that have cost the company some customers’ trust.
fullText:
On the same day that Anthropic went public in the largest IPO on record, with investor enthusiasm for the AI lab through the roof, far away at the Slush startup conference in Helsinki, the topic du jour was open source everything.

That’s the enormous opportunity being chased by companies like Fireworks AI, as enterprises seek ways to avoid paying frontier prices for their AI needs.

Four-year-old Fireworks runs AI models for other businesses. The Bay Area-based outfit specializes in open-weight models, which anyone can download, and helps customers tune them on their own data so they run faster and cheaper than the models of Anthropic, OpenAI, and other heavyweights, and are harder for rivals to copy. Customers have included Uber, Shopify, and Notion. 

Fireworks co-founder Chenyu Zhao and many others believe companies are gravitating toward platforms like his because frontier models are pricey and, in most cases, he says, unnecessary unless you need the very latest and greatest generalized intelligence. There are also growing concerns that frontier labs absorb too much of their customers’ know-how, even if only through the prompts used to get answers, a worry Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella raised in July.

Fireworks has also gotten its first black eye, having disclosed two security incidents this fall. In one, hackers reached API keys and tokens stored as secrets for a limited number of accounts; in the other, attackers breached its cloud provider, made their way into a development system, and nabbed customer data, including billing records and some datasets.

Notion says AI chat transcripts from fewer than 1% of its workspaces were exposed, but it has disconnected from Fireworks. Uber says hackers stole the names, addresses, birth dates and driver’s license numbers of about 150,000 drivers through a vendor that TechCrunch identified as Fireworks. Fireworks will have to win back the confidence of customers like them.

Fireworks, which is backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, among other firms, was assigned a $17.5 billion valuation in summer. It’s reportedly in early talks for yet another round, though Zhao declined to comment.

There’s money chasing everyone in the category, seems like. Rival companies Together AI and Baseten have announced massive rounds in recent months. On Wednesday, Palo Alto Networks said it will buy Applied Compute, which, like Fireworks, helps companies train and run custom AI models on their own data. The deal for the startup, founded just a year ago by former OpenAI researchers, is $4.5 billion, all of it in stock.

Zhao and I spoke onstage about all of it on Thursday at Slush. Here’s some of what Zhao had to say, edited for length and clarity.

You spent a decade at Google, including managing a 50-person engineering team on Google Cloud Vertex AI. Why leave when you did?

When you meet great co-founders, it’s obvious within five minutes that they’re really smart. I was sold after talking to Lin [Qiao] and Dima [Dzhulgakov]. It’s also important to find people who are genuinely nice, people you’ll enjoy working with.

How do you describe Fireworks to a CEO who has never heard of it?

I describe Fireworks as a specialized intelligence platform. OpenAI and Anthropic are building general intelligence. We use open models, which are often smaller, cheaper, and faster, and let companies add their own data to specialize them. That way you own your AI rather than being beholden to giant AI conglomerates. If you’re just using Opus or Sonnet, that’s not a differentiator.

How far behind are open models right now?

A few years ago I’d have said a year, a year and a half. Then came DeepSeek and a waterfall of fantastic open models. These days it’s at most six months behind, probably closer to three.

If the models are so close behind, why are businesses slow to switch?

Frontier models are a household brand, and before you find product-market fit, using the best model is low risk. But once you pass 10,000 or 100,000 users and you’re spending $10,000 to $100,000 a month on tokens, it’s time to think about open source.

In July, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella warned that companies using proprietary AI models pay twice, once in money and again in know-how. Do you think that warning had a material effect?

We think we’ll live in a two-model world, with frontier and open models in parallel. You want the best intelligence for high-level planning, but you don’t need a frontier model for basic arithmetic. That’s why there’s so much interest in routing, and why people now think about cost per task, not just cost per token.

Anthropic went public today. What do you think of its valuation? There’s one scenario in which it just continues to cement its place in this sort of oligopoly; there’s another where it starts to lose traction.

On the record: I’ll probably call my broker tonight and buy a few shares. This is a long-term bet. In 10 years AI usage will be at a completely different scale, and that takes an incredible amount of capital, which is why these companies are going public.

Fireworks has had a couple of security breaches recently. What do you tell customers?

Every company is probably seeing an unprecedented frequency of attacks. For our incident, a lot of the motivation was LLM jacking: hunting through providers for API keys and secrets to sell tokens on illicit marketplaces. Our promise is zero data retention for inference traffic, and there’s no indication that has been compromised.

Notion has disconnected from Fireworks. Did you lose other customers?

I don’t think I can publicly name the specific customers that were impacted. Some, such as Notion and Cursor, have gone public already. It was a small subset of our customers that had this data impact.

How did that customer data get exposed, given your zero-retention promise?

Notion was using batch prediction, where you upload a dataset that’s stored at rest, so it’s not a zero-retention product by nature. We’re moving those services to an online flow so we keep data only as long as we need it.

Jensen Huang left Nvidia last week, and Nvidia has backed Fireworks since 2024. Does that affect you?

It’s been a blow to the industry, and we feel for Jensen and his family. But Nvidia has always been a strong supporter of open source, and I don’t see that changing. We expect it to keep investing in Nemotron [Nvidia’s family of open AI models], and we’re excited to keep partnering with them.

title: At $600, the Pixel 10 is this year’s no-brainer Black Friday smartphone deal
snippet: Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a new device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list. more…
fullText:
Phones have gotten a lot more expensive over the last year or so, and it’s a trend we’re expecting to get worse before it can get better. If you’re in the market for an upgrade, this year’s Black Friday might be one of the final truly good times to buy a new device, and for just $600, last year’s Pixel 10 should be high on your list.

While buying year-old hardware typically comes with some pretty deep sacrifices between generations, that’s not particularly true with the Pixel 10 this year. From a hardware perspective, nearly everything is either identical or close enough to not particularly matter. Its design and display are all but unchanged, Qi2-ready magnets come on both models, and both devices are built with the same level of battery longevity in mind. And much to the chagrin of many a Pixel die-hard, Tensor G5 and Tensor G6 are practically interchangeable. 

Buy Google Pixel 10 at Amazon

So what are you giving up that matters? When the Pixel 11 arrived, software features made up the bulk of this list, but with last week’s Pixel Drop, a lot of the gaps between these two generations have been closed. Gemini Intelligence with Rambler, app automation, and more are in the process of rolling out to existing Pixel 10 users, and new features like Create My Widget arrived on the Pixel 10 and 11 at the exact same time. From a software perspective — Google’s bread and butter, in my eyes — the only big sacrifice comes from the year of software support that’s already complete, leaving you with just six instead of seven.

Realistically, the camera is the one place you’re likely to feel a difference. The Pixel 10 was the first non-Pro device in Google’s Tensor era to ship with a telephoto lens, but it came with some big sacrifices. The main sensor is effectively an A-series lens, and taken together, the entire package might leave something to be desired. It’s far from a bad camera though — I used it as my main shooter through most of its lifecycle — and while the Pixel 11 did get some upgrades here, I think real shutterbugs would be better off looking at Google’s Pro lineup anyway. You’ll also lose out on things like HiLight, though really, are you missing that much?

	

What makes this deal so good is really its place in the market, not as a direct comparison to the newer Pixel 11. For $600, Google’s competition is going to have a hard time competing with the value the Pixel 10 delivers. Hell, even Google might find it difficult to compete in the coming months; at full price, $600 is what the Pixel 10a goes for now, a decidedly less-impressive device compared to this model. No, this is a flagship smartphone through and through, and for $600, you’re effectively guaranteeing a reliable, powerful smartphone experience from now until 2032 — hopefully enough time for this whole RAM crisis to finally simmer down a bit.

title: Google launches Gemini 4 Neon with Carbon quality at Flash speeds, live for AI Pro
snippet: Following last week’s release of Carbon and Hydrogen, Google today is rolling out Gemini 4 Neon. The model offers “frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.” more…
fullText:
Following last week’s release of Carbon and Hydrogen, Google today is rolling out Gemini 4 Neon. The model offers “frontier-level reasoning for complex, high-frequency workflows faster and more cost efficiently.”

Before today, Google’s Gemini 4 family consisted of:

Hydrogen — Everyday help: Flash replacement

Argon — Code & analysis: “…ideal choice for the majority of software engineering and knowledge work”

Carbon — Most complex work: “…built for tasks that test the limits of a model’s intelligence”

Neon has performance comparable to, if not surpassing, Carbon across coding, reasoning, and agentic tasks, but at Flash speeds and a lower cost. 

As such, Neon is available in the Gemini app for AI Pro (and AI Ultra) subscribers, with 3.1 Pro finally going away. Neon also replaces Argon. Meanwhile, 3.5 Flash-Lite is now “Auto” in the model picker for paid users.

	

With this launch, the model picker is:

Auto: Adapts to your needs

Everyday help: 4 Hydrogen

Deeper analysis: 4 Neon

Code & complex work: 4 Carbon

In the Gemini app, Google says to expect:

Higher-quality writing and knowledge work: Neon writes clearly, with well-structured responses and a natural, direct tone. It reads uploads like spreadsheets, PDFs, and photos more precisely, turns dense material into helpful reports and summaries, and pulls in relevant details from Google apps like Gmail and Docs.

Reliable research and analysis: Neon frequently incorporates details from sources across the web to keep responses current for fast-moving topics like comparing pricing across vendors before a major purchase or pulling together a complex brief with the latest market data.

Faster help for tougher tasks: Tasks in Gemini can now run on Neon, working through complex, multi-step jobs more quickly and efficiently than with larger models. Get more done while stretching usage limits further when handing off tedious to-dos, like analyzing billing statements to spot why a utility charge spiked or cross-checking multiple receipts and documents to negotiate a refund.

	

Neon has the same 1 million-token context window with four thinking levels, like Hydrogen: Low, Medium, High, and Extra High. Officially, the new model sits between Hydrogen and Carbon in the Gemini 4 family.

Neon is built for complex coding, analytical reasoning, and production-grade enterprise workflows. While Carbon tackles your hardest, long-horizon projects and Hydrogen handles fast everyday execution, Neon balances depth and efficiency.

In terms of benchmarks:

Neon ranks ahead of comparable models and #3 overall with a score of 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its xhigh thinking level, landing just behind larger, slower models.

Neon ranks #2 on steerability (adapting cleanly to mid-task user corrections) on the new Agent Arena Index.

…reaches #1 on both the Legal Research Bench and Tax Agent Bench.

Neon also shows strong wins across categories on Surge AI, ranking #1 on most benchmarks across finance, accounting, spreadsheet modeling, and complex constraint following. 

It also scores 73.5% on Chartography for reading dense professional charts…

…performs on par with leading models on Agents’ Last Exam v1.1 (75.8%). 

It achieves #1 overall on both Zapier’s AutomationBench (56.3%) and Andon Labs’ Vending-Bench 2 ($16,843), a long-horizon simulation of running a business. 

…it debuts #2 globally with a score of 1336 on Arena’s new Agent Arena Index across 4,200+ real-world agent sessions.

Neon is best in class on Terminal-Bench Science (70.5%), RiemannBench (84.0%), and HLE-Diamond (71.3%).

…ranking #1 overall on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index (58.6)

score of 65.2% on Terminal-Bench 4.1

46.2% (at its default high setting) on FrontierCode 2.0.

Neon is priced at $3/1M input tokens and $15/1M output tokens, or twice as expensive as Hydrogen. Argon and Carbon cost $2/1M input and $10/1M output until November 30. After the promotional pricing, it will be $4/1M input and $20/1M output, with Neon 25% cheaper as a result.

The model is also available in Google Antigravity for paid AI Pro or Ultra subscribers.

title: Canva introduces new controls to hide generative AI features
snippet: In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In light of growing pushback from users who want more control over how AI is integrated into their apps (if at all), Canva is introducing new settings that let them hide generative AI features and see less AI-generated content. Here are the details.

Canva adds an off switch for generative AI

Canva today announced new controls that will let Free and Pro users choose whether to see generative AI features across the app, as well as how much AI-generated content appears in search results and in recommendations for templates and design elements.

The company notes that both controls are available at no additional cost and can be turned on or off at any time.

According to Canva, “the future of creativity isn’t a choice between AI and no AI.” For this reason, it is introducing the following controls:

Generative AI feature control. A new switch to turn supported generative AI features on or off. When it’s off, those features are hidden across Canva, and can be switched back on any time. It can be found under Profile > Settings > Permissions > then switch Enable generative AI features on or off.

AI-generated content control. A new option to see less AI-generated content while browsing the Canva library, without changing any existing designs. It can be found Profile > Your account > AI personalization, and enable showing less AI-generated content.

The company says that, while it knows that there is an ongoing debate between users with opposing views on whether AI has a place in creative work, it thinks “both views are valid”:

“It’s not our place to tell anyone how to create, so today we’re launching two new controls that put that decision firmly with our community […].”

Importantly, the company noted that select features that use AI without generating new content will remain available even when generative AI features are turned off:

“Some of Canva’s everyday editing tools use AI to make simple tasks faster, without generating anything new. Background Remover, one of Canva’s most popular tools, lifts a subject cleanly out of a photo in a single click, and Magic Grab lets creators select an object in an image and move it somewhere else in the design. Both remain available when the generative AI switch is off, because they work only with what’s already in a design.”

Canva added that these tools also won’t add an AI label to a design’s metadata, since that label is reserved for AI-generated content.

As for the company’s design content library, Canva said that while “a small portion of the library is AI-generated content made by Canva, including some abstract backgrounds and illustrated graphics,” its community has told it “they want an easier way to find design assets made by real people, so the content control reduces the number of AI-generated templates and elements that appear in search results and recommendations.”

With today’s announcement, Canva is essentially expanding on the AI permissions already available to administrators of Business, Enterprise, Teams, and Education accounts, which let organizations control how their teams use AI.

title: Signal is blocking Gemini and Siri AI from reading your screen
snippet: Signal users on iOS will see this option to toggle blocking screenshots and preventing Siri AI from scanning on-screen content. | Image: Signal Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users' messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are "undermining Signal's ability to independently guarantee privacy," Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access. "We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal - and application developers beyond - lack robust tools to prevent AI age … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
Signal is restricting the ability to take screenshots on Android and iOS devices in an effort to prevent AI agents from reading users’ messages and other data. The agentic AI capabilities built into operating systems that analyze on-screen information to learn more about the user are “undermining Signal’s ability to independently guarantee privacy,” Signal president Meredith Whittaker said in a blog post, while urging OS providers to make it easier for app developers to control what data agents can access.

“We want to be very clear: it is a serious problem that Signal – and application developers beyond – lack robust tools to prevent AI agents from undermining application-level privacy,” Whittaker said. “Even where we are able to detect and block AI data access, Google, Apple, Microsoft, and others do not provide ways for developers to easily restrict such AI data access without making drastic compromises to the core user experience. This is also the reason we are currently unable to implement these protections on macOS.”

Signal is addressing the privacy concerns by blocking the ability to take screenshots in the app on iOS 27 and Android, which should prevent Siri, Gemini, and other Android AI assistants from reading on-screen content. Users can restore screenshot capabilities in Signal’s app settings, but Whittaker warns that doing so will “potentially expose your (and your contacts’) Signal content to these AI agents, and break our privacy guarantees.” Whittaker admits that Signal’s screenshot-blocking remedy is “incomplete,” as it doesn’t address alternative ways that AI agents can access app data, such as retrieving it via the device file system.

Signal took a similar approach last year to prevent Microsoft’s controversial Recall feature from capturing secured chats. The encrypted messaging service says it’s struggling to develop a better solution due to the lack of available information regarding how AI agents are actually accessing application data, and is now calling on Apple, Google, and Microsoft to provide “simple technical tools and accurate documentation” to app developers. Signal also says more tools are needed to prevent third-party agents, like Meta’s Muse, from using deep accessibility settings in apps like a “skeleton key” to access application data.

“We all need to recognize that the current integration of AI agents into the operating system, without these common-sense remedies, represents an existential threat to privacy at the application layer, and the ability of independent developers like Signal to protect your sensitive data,” said Whittaker. “Signal is the canary in the coal mine, but this affects the entire ecosystem and should galvanize anyone who cares about these fundamental rights.”

title: Material 3 Expressive adds scrolling time picker, AI Studio upgrades Android app creation
snippet: Google has given the time picker component a Material 3 Expressive redesign, while adding a new scrolling variant. Meanwhile, Google AI Studio is boosting its Android app development experience. more…
fullText:
Google has given the time picker component a Material 3 Expressive redesign, while adding a new scrolling variant. Meanwhile, Google AI Studio is boosting its Android app development experience.

Compared to Material 3, the updated M3 Expressive input and dial time pickers drop the “Select time” hint in the top-right corner, while the AM and PM buttons now benefit from expressive shape, color, and behavior. The hour and minute fields, as well as the dial selector, feature higher contrast.

Old vs. new (input & dial)

The big addition today is the scroll time picker. Instead of using the keyboard or analog clock to pick the time, you can just vertically scroll when setting an alarm or scheduling an event. 

	
	

The Material Design team says this “compact way to select time” is “best placed inline with other content.” A keyboard icon lets you switch to the input time picker. 

Use scroll time pickers instead of dial pickers when you want people to see surrounding content.

You can see various examples below:

Google today also introduced scroll fields to select different units of measurement, like distance, weight, or temperature. In a health app, they can be used for water, calories, and more.

In other related developments, building an Android app in Google AI Studio got an upgrade today. The updates include:

Full-stack persistence and sign-in: Automatically provision a Cloud Firestore database with Security Rules and Google Sign-In so user data syncs across sessions and devices.

Secure Gemini API calls: Call Gemini models from your Android app without exposing API keys in your APK, protected by Firebase AI Logic and Firebase App Check.

Personal Google Play publishing: Ship Android apps directly to your personal Google Play library with a standard Google account and install them on your phone in clicks.

Faster, high-definition emulator with audio: Spin up Android emulators with lower latency, toggle HD video streaming, and test real-time audio output directly in your browser.

One-click screenshot to agent: Capture a live frame from the running emulator with a single click and attach it to your prompt to guide visual UI edits.

Custom fonts and Android CLI integration: Style Jetpack Compose UIs with custom typography, backed under the hood by the official Android CLI for reliable project scaffolding and builds.

title: The UK and some other countries don’t get more Siri AI usage with iCloud+
snippet: Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan. However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances … more…
fullText:
Apple this week revealed the additional Siri AI usage you’ll get if you have an iCloud+ subscription. This ranges from doubled limits for a 200GB plan to 20 times for a 12TB plan.

However, the company’s support document reveals that some countries will not get access to these increased usage allowances …

Increased Siri AI usage

Apple hasn’t yet specified the standard limits applicable to Siri AI usage, instead saying that these will vary depending on anything from the feature used to the overall level of demand at the time. However, it did list the proportional increases you get with paid iCloud plans.

Some countries excluded

However, tucked away in the small print in the company’s support document are some exclusions. One of them is no surprise: EU countries. 

Siri AI isn’t available at all in the EU due to Apple’s perception of potential antitrust issues. Essentially, Apple believes that if it launches Siri AI there, it will be required to give competing AI services the same level of access to its devices. But three other countries are specifically excluded:

Brazil

South Korea

The UK

Apple gives no explanation, simply saying:

Increased access to Siri AI with iCloud+ is subject to Siri AI availability and is not available in Brazil, the EU, UK, or South Korea.

However, I have a strong suspicion about the reason.

My theory

What all three countries have in common is that they’ve taken a strong antitrust stance with Apple on a number of occasions over a range of issues.

It may be that Apple has genuine concerns about how regulators might respond if they effectively throw in free access to increased Siri AI usage. The company may fear that this would be viewed as anti-competitive by implicitly disadvantaging other AI services.

A less charitable take would be that Apple is firing a warning shot across the bows of these countries, seeking to communicate that there are consequences for what it views as attacks on its ecosystem. If customers are angered by missing out, Apple might be hoping that these feelings would be directed at regulators rather than the iPhone maker.

title: New Gemini setting lets you keep chat history, but turn off AI training
snippet: Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.” more…
fullText:
Google is rolling out new privacy settings for the Gemini app that will let you “keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.”

Gemini’s existing Keep Activity setting “controls how long your chats are saved and whether they are used to train generative AI models.”

Google is now separating that preference into two new options. 

	

The first setting is called “History” and lets you “control how long your history is saved.” If disabled:

	

“…future chats will be saved for around 2 months and used to respond to you, process your feedback, and protect Google, its users, and the public, with help from human reviewers.”

The duration is currently 24 hours for chat context, and 72 hours to help protect Google, users, and the public. 

The second setting allows you to “separately control whether your chat content, including text and attachments, is used to train generative AI models.”

With this change, you will be able to keep your history while independently controlling generative AI model training.

If Keep Activity is currently off, the two “new settings will both be off.” These changes are rolling out over the “coming weeks,” and Google is notifying users via email.

title: Google Fi app redesign brings floating toolbar & Ask Fi
snippet: Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign. more…
fullText:
Google Fi Wireless is the latest first-party app to adopt a floating toolbar as part of a small navigation redesign.

Previously, the companion app still used a tall Material 3 bottom bar. With the network switching update announced last week, Google Fi now has a floating navigation toolbar.

The tabs remain Home, Plan, Billing, Shop, and Support. A pill-shaped tab indicator is leveraged, while there’s a prominent shadow effect. Given the floating nature, you see what’s around the toolbar, while Fi Wireless now extends underneath the system navigation bar.

However, the Shop tab loads a webpage as before, resulting in a gap and wasted space. 

	

There’s now a floating action button for the new Google AI-powered Ask Fi chatbot. It provides “instant account help and troubleshooting.” If you ask for human support, the contents of the conversation carry over. 

This redesign is rolling out with version 171 of the app as a server-side update. Google Fi joins Google Photos, Chat, and Pixel Now Playing in adopting floating navigation, which is likely the new first-party mandate for a more edge-to-edge design.

Secondary network switching is not yet widely available, with Google telling us last week that it’s a gradual rollout. The MVNO is also ending Pixel exclusivity for Wi-Fi Auto Connect+ with availability on “select” Samsung and Motorola phones.

title: OpenAI begins testing dots with ChatGPT Plus users, expands Business access
snippet: Following its launch for ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise users, OpenAI is now beginning to test ChatGPT dot with a small number of ChatGPT Plus subscribers. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Following its launch for ChatGPT Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise users, OpenAI is now beginning to test ChatGPT dot with a small number of ChatGPT Plus subscribers. Here are the details.

Dots are coming to ChatGPT Plus users

In September, OpenAI announced ChatGPT dot, an always-on, proactive assistant that can handle ongoing tasks, work across connected apps, and make progress on projects even when users aren’t actively interacting with it.

With its initial availability limited to Pro, Business Premium, and Enterprise plans, OpenAI explained that conversations with ChatGPT dots don’t count toward regular ChatGPT usage limits for Pro and Business Premium subscribers, although more complex tasks are subject to separate allowances.

Additionally, any work delegated to ChatGPT Work or Codex counts toward the allowances for those products.

Here’s OpenAI’s original announcement on how ChatGPT dot works:

Dots are frontier intelligence that have your back. Powered by GPT-6 Astra, they have their own cloud computer, learn from feedback over time, and can work towards your goals 24/7. Through our ecosystem of plugins, they can readily connect to over 4,000 apps, giving them the tools to help wherever you need them.

Since then, OpenAI has expanded the range of models powering ChatGPT dot, adding GPT-6.1 Terra alongside GPT-6 Astra earlier this month.

The company has also introduced several new features, including iOS widgets and Shortcuts integration, the ability to communicate with Dots through iMessage and RCS on Android (currently in beta for Pro subscribers in the US), and support for replying directly from iOS notifications.

More recently, OpenAI added custom instructions, allowing users to specify how their Dots should behave and respond.

Today, OpenAI’s Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux, who leads engineering for Codex and ChatGPT, announced that the company will start expanding dots availability to Plus subscribers (though for now this will be a limited test), in addition to rolling it out to all ChatGPT Business Standard users:

Heads up, we’re starting to test dots with a small number of ChatGPT Plus users. Looking forward to the continued feedback as we expand and I’m recently seeing a lot more positives around how good the proactivity has been after many improvements. 

We’re also bringing dots to all…

— Tibo (@thsottiaux) November 19, 2026

It’s not yet clear whether ChatGPT Plus and Business Standard users will have the same Dots usage allowances as subscribers on higher-tier plans, or whether additional restrictions will apply, though that should become clearer as the rollout progresses.

title: Bending Spoons buys Mailchimp for $3.68 billion
snippet: Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it looks like Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain.
fullText:
Bending Spoons has bought up another distressed internet company. This time, it’s the email marketing firm Mailchimp, bought for $3.68 billion from the tax-preparation giant Intuit. 

Intuit acquired the company in 2021 for roughly $12 billion, so it’s taking quite a loss — and, perhaps, Bending Spoons is getting quite a bargain. At the time of the sale to Intuit, that acquisition caused headlines because Mailchimp employees reportedly received no equity, so no share of the sale proceeds, because the founders had allegedly promised them they didn’t need it as they would never sell.

Flash forward to now with Intuit hit hard by the Death Star to SaaS trade — aka AI — with the company’s shares worth less than half what they were a year ago. The company told Reuters that the sale will let it sharpen its focus on AI tools for small businesses, and the new cash will be used to repurchase shares.

Bending Spoons describes the transaction as an all-cash deal, although that’s not quite true: As part of the same package, Intuit is buying $368 million in newly minted shares of Bending Spoons, so the net effect is a split of 90% cash to 10% stock.

Still, the transaction is a major pickup for Bending Spoons, which has become a kind of clearinghouse for late-stage web properties, with its game plan to hold them long term. In just the last year, the company has snapped up AOL, Eventbrite, Airtable and Miro. Previous acquisitions include older stalwarts like Evernote, Meetup and Vimeo. In each case, Bending Spoons integrated the products into centralized engineering and revenue systems, resulting in significant cost savings while often improving the available support and product resources.

“We want to place ourselves as an operator that takes beloved brands and makes them much better,” Bending Spoons co-founder and chief product officer, Matteo Danieli, told TechCrunch in July.

title: Amid Anthropic’s IPO, Google, Microsoft and OpenAI Drop New AI Models
snippet: With the focus on Nvidia and Anthropic, several new models were released by OpenAI and Microsoft.
fullText:
It’s been a wild week for the AI industry — and it’s only Thursday. Aside from outages, cheating scandals and Anthropic’s pending IPO, there are several new models available now. Google dropped Gemini 4 Neon, Microsoft dropped seven new versions of its MAI models at its Ignite conference, and OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, the next step forward for its flagship models.

First, Google: The tech titan dropped Gemini 4 Neon, its latest flagship model. Besides continuing its trend of naming the Gemini 4 family of models after elements from the periodic table, Gemini 4 Neon boasts better speeds for complex tasks and scientific work. It’s available now for paying Google AI subscribers and developers.

Next, Microsoft: At its Ignite developer conference on Tuesday, Microsoft introduced seven new AI models. They include MAI Cyber 2 Flash, MAI Code 2, MAI Image 2.7 and Dragon Copilot Transcribe — models meant to help with tasks in cybersecurity, coding, image generation and transcription.

			

More from CNET

It’s clear from Microsoft’s marketing that it is aiming to position its new tech as a cheaper alternative to OpenAI’s and Anthropic’s leading models, with many of these significantly cheaper to run at the enterprise level. That, plus its new licensed weight program, which lets companies customize the new AI models for their purposes, highlights how Microsoft is continuing to pitch its AI tech to the workplace.

And let’s not forget OpenAI: The ChatGPT maker dropped two new model variants of its flagship model, GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol. Astra is the big model — it costs the most and uses the most firepower to handle complex tasks — and Sol is the “everyday” version. Both models beat their sibling models in OpenAI’s benchmarking. These are available to paying subscribers in ChatGPT and Codex globally now. (Disclosure: Ziff Davis, CNET’s parent company, in 2025 filed a lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

The AI elephant in the room

While these new models might be useful for AI power users, they are far from most of the AI industry’s mind this week. During Tuesday’s earnings call, new interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress tried to assure investors that everything was “business as usual” after weeks of turmoil inside the company rocked the global economy. Nvidia cofounder and now-former CEO Jensen Huang’s multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence, threw the company into chaos and have attracted the attention of the Securities and Exchange Commission and both chambers of Congress, where Huang has agreed to testify.

And then there’s Anthropic. The Claude maker is becoming a public company this week, with the possible biggest-ever IPO. Anthropic had an opening price of $83 per share, valuing it at $1.5 trillion — narrowly surpassing the valuation of Elon Musk’s mega-conglomerate, SpaceX, at its record-setting IPO earlier this year (now with SpaceXSI, because President Donald Trump said so).

The Nvidia scandal caused a drastic 14% dip in its stock price during its first week and wiped out $1 trillion in the company’s value, but Anthropic investors don’t seem to be worried. At least, not publicly.

If nothing else, Anthropic’s IPO and the new models from Google, OpenAI and Microsoft are stark reminders that the tech industry is nowhere near ready to slow down on AI. Even as financial, environmental and legal concerns mount — and arguably hit a fever pitch during the midterm elections — Big Tech is plowing ahead with generative AI.

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katelyn Chedraoui
						

						

							Reporter 2						
					

											

								

											Katelyn is a reporter with CNET covering artificial intelligence, including chatbots, image and video generators. Her work explores how new AI technology is infiltrating our lives, shaping the content we consume on social media and affecting the people behind the screens. title: Google AI Mode rolling out temporary threads
snippet: Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small update to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history. more…
fullText:
Following last week’s Gemini 4 Hydrogen launch, a small update to AI Mode today lets you start a “temporary thread” that won’t be saved to your Google history.

Like in the Gemini app, anything you discuss in a temporary thread isn’t saved to your account. It won’t appear in conversation history or influence future recommendations.

These AI Mode responses won’t be personalized with past preferences. After you close a temporary thread, there’s no way to access it again.

To launch, tap the new pen button with a dotted border in the top-right corner, which is the same icon used in the Gemini app. The personalized greeting at the top of the prompt box switches to “Welcome, stranger.”

	

This is an alternative to opening google.com in Incognito Mode, while still being able to use the model picker. Meanwhile, Google’s use of “threads” to describe AI Mode conversations versus “chats” in the Gemini app is interesting.

Temporary threads are rolling out globally starting today on mobile and desktop browsers across all AI Mode languages.

This joins other changes that Google is still testing for AI Mode. With the latest Google app beta on Android, you can now quickly upload from Google Drive, which joins Gallery, Camera, and Files as attachment options. You can also now access Canvas on Android.

title: Anthropic’s IPO could deliver $156B to charity
snippet: At a stock price of $95, the frontier lab's Public Benefit Foundation, its employee donations, and the company's match tot up to $156 billion.
fullText:
Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO has made quite a few people generationally wealthy, but it will also be an enormous windfall for the causes backed by the frontier lab and its employees. 

As you might expect from a company whose leadership emerged from the world of effective altruism (EA), Anthropic has multiple different avenues for cash raised in its market debut to be directed to philanthropy.

First, the company’s Public Benefit Fund, or PBF (analogous to OpenAI’s foundation), was allotted 5% of the company’s shares, almost 850 million. At the current trading price of about $95, that will leave it with an endowment of $80 billion. And if the company continues its astonishing growth rate, Anthropic could add further 2% increases every time the company’s valuation grows more than 50% over the IPO price of $83, or about $124.50 per share for the next threshold.

The PBF’s money will be focused on research and activities related to increasing the benefit of artificial intelligence to humanity. The first commitment of the PBF was $200 million to study the impact of AI on workers; Anthropic has said it will consider donations to philanthropic organizations or “direct distributions to specific populations” — perhaps a hint of future UBI plans.

Anthropic also donated $50 million to the city of San Francisco last week. A company spokesperson tells TechCrunch the donation did not come from the PBF.

Next, Anthropic’s employees have pledged shares to philanthropic causes of their choice, and the company will match those donations 3-to-1 for longer tenured employees and 1-to-1 for newer ones. In its S-1 filing, the company said that it had reserved more than 550 million shares to fulfill pledges made before September 30.

Working backwards from that figure, and based on the disclosure that 84% of the shares were reserved for early employee matches, we can estimate that employees have pledged $23 billion of donations; the company’s match on those would be roughly $53 billion, depending on the stock price when those matches are delivered.

All told, it adds up to $156 billion — a huge amount of potential philanthropy. For context, Americans donated $617 billion to charity in 2025; if all of the pledged funds resulting from today’s transactions get to do-gooders, that will be equal to about a quarter of all U.S. donations made last year.

Employees will need to make good on their pledges for this to work out, and the value of the match will ultimately depend on when Anthropic makes its donation. The shares could also go to donor-advised funds, which would likely limit their initial impact.

Interviews with employees and institutions suggest that donors are most likely to support EA-inflected charities like Longview Philanthropy, GiveWell, Coefficient Giving, Foresight Institute, and Giving What We Can. And it seems likely that significant funding will be allocated to AI safety research, given the concerns expressed about that subject by many Anthropic employees.

title: Apple memory suppliers expect price increases through at least 2030 [U]
snippet: Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand. Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases. more…
fullText:
Key Apple memory supplier SK Hynix has warned that RAM and flash memory shortages are likely to last through at least 2030, keeping product prices high. Apple is believed to be one of 14 customers who have locked in priority orders, but the contract does not protect against price increases related to the balance of supply and demand.

Update: Apple is reportedly about to sign a similar contract with Samsung, also permitting market-driven price increases.

SK Hynix says that while AI continues to drive demand and growth, there is little that can be done in the short to medium term to increase supply.

Supply, on the other hand, is not keeping pace with the growth of the market. Given technical difficulty of leading-edge processes and the long lead time required to build new production facilities, it expects the structure in which demand exceeds supply to persist through 2030.

The Register reports that SK Hynix has long-term deals with 14 tech giants for priority orders, but these allow for market-based price increases.

14 big buyers […] will collectively buy more than half of its output during 2027 and 2028, and some of them want to extend those agreements. The Korean giant doesn’t mind that because the deals include “a mechanism that reflects market conditions within a price range agreed upon with customers”

Apple is used to being in the driving seat when it comes to negotiating with suppliers, but this is not the case where memory and flash storage is concerned. Here, the shortages mean that it will have been forced to agree to contracts that allow significant price hikes in order to obtain guaranteed supplies.

Nikkei Asia also reports that printed circuit boards may be the next component to experience constrained supply. Once a humble commodity item, advances in the technology has turned them into specialist tech, with more layers and higher bandwidth requirements. The report says “that complexity shrinks the supplier pool and extends lead times.”

Apple said back in June that the company was doing its best to mitigate the price increases, but it has so far been unable to do so.

title: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price
snippet: Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, representing more than $80 billion in new capital raised.
fullText:
In Brief

Posted:

8:59 AM PST · November 19, 2026

Image Credits:Michael Nagle/Bloomberg / Getty Images

		

							

											
									

					

	

Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.

Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.

The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch, “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.”

The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft.

In a speech before the opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.”

title: MacPaw’s Moonlock comes to iPhone, helping users detect potential scams
snippet: After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
After launching Moonlock for Mac last year, MacPaw is bringing its scam-detection app to iPhone today. Here are the details.

Moonlock now available for iPhone

When MacPaw launched Moonlock on the Mac, the company described its new app as something that “complements Apple’s built-in security tools, protects from Mac-specific malware, and helps you understand cybersecurity better.”

In practice, the Mac app includes real-time protection against potential threats. Users can also manually scan their Mac for malware, including suspicious files hidden in system folders and email attachments.

Beyond that, Moonlock includes a VPN to encrypt internet traffic, a network inspector that shows where apps are sending data and lets users block connections to specific countries, and an AI-powered scam detector that analyzes messages pasted into the app for signs of phishing. It also helps users review and adjust macOS security settings.

Today, MacPaw is launching Moonlock for iPhone, a move the company says “helps people recognize potential scams, understand their iPhone’s security and take practical steps to improve it.”

Unlike the Mac version, Moonlock for iPhone doesn’t scan for malware, as iOS prevents third-party apps from accessing other apps and their files. Instead, it focuses on identifying potential scams, checking for exposed personal information, and helping users improve their iPhone’s security.

On the iPhone, Moonlock lets users quickly check suspicious texts, screenshots, and QR codes for phishing, in addition to checking whether their email addresses have appeared in known data breaches.

As MacPaw explains it, Moonlock’s Scam Detect “helps people check suspicious messages they encounter throughout the day. Whether it’s a text message, a screenshot shared by a friend, or a QR code, users can paste, scan or share content directly with Moonlock and receive an assessment explaining why something may be suspicious.”

Here’s Oleg Stukalenko, Head of Product Management at Moonlock by MacPaw, on today’s launch:

“When we launched Moonlock, our goal was to make cybersecurity something anyone could understand and use. But so much of what people do today, from banking to everyday conversations, happens on their phones. Bringing Moonlock to iPhone felt like the natural next step. We want to help people spot a scam before they tap, see where their security stands, and know exactly what to do next.”

MacPaw adds that Moonlock for iPhone also includes the following features:

Safe SMS: Automatically filters suspected scam texts out of the inbox when enabled, with a record of what was caught and why.

Security Score: Provides a score from 0 to 100 reflecting the iPhone’s security setup, along with one recommended action at a time to help users improve it.

Email Breach History: Tells users if their email has turned up in a known data breach, which service leaked it, when and what was exposed, then walks them through securing each affected account.

Device and Network Checks: Helps users review Wi-Fi safety, passcode protection, iOS updates and signs of jailbreaking. A checklist of recommended one-time fixes provides step-by-step instructions and an estimate of how long each change takes.

MacPaw’s Moonlock for iPhone is free to download, with subscriptions available for $9.99 per month or $49.99 per year.
