title: Apple hears Liquid Glass feedback, tests small but welcome change
snippet: Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale. Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling … more…
fullText:
Liquid Glass was one of the most controversial and polarizing UI changes Apple has made for a long time. The company listened to the feedback and made a number of changes, the most significant of which was to introduce a sliding transparency scale.

Apple is currently testing a change some will consider insignificant but I personally find very welcome: softer edges when scrolling … 

	

Apple’s introduction of the Liquid Glass UI split the Apple community, some hailing it as one of the best improvements seen for many years, and others rejecting it as a usability disaster.

As is often the case with any change, the controversy dampened significantly once people had a chance to get used to it. That is not the same as everyone being happy with it, however. Apple later tried to please most of the people most of the time with a slider that allows people to customize the level of transparency, from a very frosted glass look to an almost completely clear one.

Code sleuth pdfu has spotted that the company is currently testing a small but welcome additional choice.

They heard the feedback: Apple is testing the return of iOS 26’s softer scroll-edge effect in navigation bars when glass tint is set to 25% or lower.

Currently disabled behind UIKit/clear_glass_soft_pocket. Applies to the default/auto style. pic.twitter.com/D2NvKfESYa

— pdfu (@itspdfu) November 16, 2026

The difference is somewhat subtle, and some may consider it irrelevant, but as someone who has transparency maxed-out I’m a fan of the softer fade and would welcome the option to be able to reinstate this.

title: Calling in sick: Vice City
snippet: Good morning. Today I’m TKTK… more…
fullText:
Good morning. Today I’m TKTK…

Inbox is the tech newsletter that goes beyond the news cycle. We cover the most important 9to5Google stories from the last couple of days along with a few highlights from around the web. We publish every Tuesday and Thursday, and if you like what you read, please subscribe.

Inbox is written by Daniel Bader. Read previous issues here, and then catch up with Ben Schoon’s excellent Weekender column published every Sunday.

⭐️ Starred

Not sure if you’ve heard, but the biggest video game of all time is out today: buying Anthropic stock. Yes, in case you haven’t already blown all of your money on the GTA VI Ultimate Edition, you can try your luck at buying one of the most anticipated IPOs of all time when ANT goes public on the Nasdaq later today.

	

But you’re likely up, playing the game that is, according to Metacritic, already among the best of all time. It’s currently sitting at a near-perfect 99/100 on the aggregator, with reviewers calling it “a masterpiece” and “gaming’s… greatest love story.” It’s a game in which you can do basically anything you want, from the violent to the vacuous. 

More than anything, though, I’m just excited to discover all the different ways the game allows you to find and consume coffee.

As I’m sure happened in every newsroom, the conversation this week turned to whether traffic will meaningfully decline today as up to 1.5 million people “call in sick” to play GTA VI. If you’ve been awake since the crack of dawn trying to meander your way to Vice City, you’re just one of many folks experiencing the rarest of moments in 2026: a singular, unifying cultural event.

My biggest question isn’t whether gamers will play GTA VI but whether normies will. Previous games in the series, particularly GTA V, sold hundreds of millions of copies and still draw countless players today. GTA VI feels even more inviting to those who just want to spend time in its sandbox to do some fishing, dancing, or flying. One reviewer even called it a “cozy game” where he just spent time walking around a zoo.

While the size, scale, and impact of GTA VI are exponentially higher, the last time I heard people talking about a game in this way was during the pandemic, when everyone was hunkering down for a winter of Animal Crossing.

By the way, GTA VI has a functioning smartphone that can be used for making calls, sending texts, taking photos, looking at “Instagram,” and setting reminders, among other things. It’s yet another minor detail in a game full of them. Plus, it looks like an original Pixel.

title: Apple fires back at Epic over claims it withheld 122,000 documents
snippet: Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
Apple has responded to Epic Games’ filing from last Friday, pushing back against accusations that it improperly withheld more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions. Here are the details.

A bit of background

While the Supreme Court is set to review whether the civil contempt designation against Apple should be upheld in its lawsuit against Epic Games, the two companies have also been battling in the district court over what commission, if any, Apple should be allowed to charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

Apple submitted its proposal to the district court on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, but Epic is disputing not just the basis for those proposed rates, but also Apple’s handling of document production in the proceedings.

As part of the proceedings, Epic had submitted 16 categories of documents it wanted Apple to produce (including “internal analyses of the financial or business impact” of its proposed commissions and “communications relating to any strategies to dissuade developers from offering link-outs”), along with a list of current and former Apple employees whose records should be searched.

Apple agreed to use Epic’s proposed search terms and include all employees, and began producing documents it determined were responsive to Epic’s requests.

Epic, however, said last Friday that Apple was improperly withholding more than 122,000 documents matching those search terms from the records of the seven initial employees, and asked the court to order Apple to produce all matching non-privileged documents, regardless of its relevance assessments.

Which brings us to Apple’s newest filing.

Apple’s newest filing

In its filing, Apple argues that contrary to Epic’s claim that its proposed search terms were “tailored” to the proceedings over link-out fees, they were actually “overbroad,” capturing large numbers of unrelated documents.

For instance, Apple notes that while intended to identify documents related to its proposed commission rates, Epic’s “commission*” search term also “captures documents that refer to government and private commissions, as well as documents hitting on the totally irrelevant term ‘commissioner,’ such as documents discussing the NFL Commissioner.”

As Apple explains it:

“[…] the use of a wildcard in a search string is designated by the asterisk symbol, which means that the search string will hit on any term that includes the prefix before the asterisk.

In the same vein, Apple notes that “Epic’s use of ‘fee*’ in its search strings related to litigation and Apple’s link-out-related projects pulled in documents containing words like ‘feel,’ ‘feed,’ ‘feedback,’ ‘feet,’ and ‘feeble’ without the word ‘fee’ or ‘fees’ appearing at all.”

Apple’s overall argument is that these unrelated matches account for the vast majority of documents identified by Epic’s searches, and it cites legal precedent to argue that it should only be required to produce documents responsive to Epic’s requests, rather than every document matching the agreed-upon search terms:

In fact, at least 95% of the Initial Custodian Document Population hit on generic terms like these and did not include any reference to the term “link-out” or its variations, despite that concept being central to the Proffer and related discovery. These sweeping terms do not just increase the total volume of the Initial Custodian Document Population, they also captured highly sensitive and irrelevant documents, such as Apple employees’ personal tax or financial records, medical records, documents discussing unannounced products, documents containing passwords, investor-relations materials, and privileged or protected legal communications.

And

The law is clear: parties are only required to produce responsive documents, not every document returned by a search string. […] (“The Court will not compel defendants to produce any document simply because it contains a search term whether or not it is responsive to the discovery request.”). Epic has not shown, and cannot show, why the regular discovery process should be disrupted here. Speculation based on hit counts, particularly where the producing party can explain low responsiveness rates, does not justify the extraordinary and unprecedented remedy Epic seeks.

Apple goes on to argue that complying with Epic’s demands would require extensive additional work, including reviewing documents for privileged or sensitive information and redacting protected material, making it impossible to meet Epic’s proposed December 2 deadline.

Finally, Apple asks the court to reject Epic’s motion but proposes that, should the court decide that some intervention is warranted, a randomized, statistically significant sample of the documents it deems nonresponsive be submitted to a Special Master for independent review, rather than producing all of them to Epic directly.

title: Polaroid’s Portable Printer Got Me Right Back Into Journaling
snippet: Polaroid’s little photo printer helps me quickly save memories with superb photo quality.
fullText:
Polaroid’s Hi-Print 2×3 printer.Nicole Lee

I loved journaling as a child. It helped me survive hormonal changes, the usual teen dramas, plus a hefty dose of existential angst. Then college called, and I moved to a different country, leaving behind my childhood, my Nirvana cassettes (I’m old, OK?) and, sadly, my journaling habit.

I made multiple attempts to return to journaling throughout the years, with varying success. I’ve delved into bullet journals under the pretense of improving my productivity, but I gave up when it became too much effort. I’ve invested in multiple notebooks and planners, only to eventually neglect them. 

Recently, however, I found a way for me to actually stick to the habit: a $110 Polaroid Hi-Print pocket printer. 

			

More from CNET

It all began when I discovered the wondrous world of journaling TikTok. In short-form videos, creators would show off beautiful journal pages decorated with colored markers, stickers, washi tape and, yes, photos — specifically photos from portable printers because the prints are small enough to fit within the confines of a typical journal or planner. I really liked the idea of decking out my journal pages with photos of my everyday life. I knew I had to get one. 

After a bit of research, I decided on a couple of criteria. First, I wanted the printer to be a dye sublimation printer rather than a ZINK (Zero Ink) printer. Dye sublimation printers essentially use heat to transfer dye onto the paper, while ZINK printers use a special paper that activates under heat with no ink required (hence the name). Dye sublimation prints tend to be higher quality because it transfers the dye in layers of cyan, magenta and yellow, followed by a protective coating. 

Second, I wanted the photo to be on sticky paper so that I didn’t have to mess around with glue to add these photos to my journal. 

I found quite a number of dye sublimation pocket printers on the market, but the one that caught my eye immediately was the Polaroid Hi-Print 2×3 Generation 2 pocket printer. I fell in love with it the moment I saw it. The sleek white design, the Polaroid logo and that curved rainbow accent on the edge really sealed the deal for me. Call me a sucker for style, I guess.

Photos are printed after multiple passes, starting with a yellow layer.Nicole Lee/CNET

I purchased a Hi-Print 2×3 “starter set,” which includes the printer along with two 2×3 paper cartridges. Each cartridge has 10 photo sheets, and each sheet is made out of sticky back photo paper, which is exactly what I wanted. Both the Gen 2 and the prior Gen 1 are easy to find; the main difference is the newer one uses a USB-C charging port while the original uses the older Micro-USB port.

Getting started with the printer is simple enough: Download the Polaroid Hi-Print app, pair the printer with your phone and you’re ready to go. The app is fairly easy to navigate. I like that it lets you arrange your photos in collages so you’re not limited to just one photo per sheet. You can also decorate your prints with colorful frames or decorations. The printer even offers a mosaic option that lets you print out one big image using multiple sheets. 

A protective coating finishes off the photo.Nicole Lee/CNET

Since it’s a dye sublimation printer, the Hi-Print prints out photos in stages. It lays down the different colors in multiple passes (yellow in the first pass, magenta in the second pass, and so forth). Because of that, printing does take a while: around 60 seconds per photo. 

But I don’t mind the delay, as the resulting photo quality is superb. The colors are vibrant and the overall image is nice and sharp. The contrast could be a little better, but for a little pocket printer, the quality definitely exceeded my expectations. 

There are a few downsides, however. The obvious one is that photo cartridges can be pretty expensive. One pack of 20 sheets is around $17, though you can get it for $14 each if you buy the 5-pack. That’s still almost 70 cents per 2×3 print. If you use multiple prints, that can add up pretty quickly. 

Thanks to the Polaroid printer, my journal is now a photo album too.Nicole Lee/CNET

Another downside is that it doesn’t have a super long battery life. It only has a 620mAh battery, which Polaroid says will last up to 20 photo printing sessions. I only ever use this printer at home, so this isn’t a big deal for me, but I can see this being a potential disappointment if you want to bring this printer on the road. That said, if you do want to charge it, it doesn’t take that long. Polaroid says it takes under an hour, and that feels about right based on my experience. 

I’ve had this printer for a few months now, and I’m very pleased with it. Since I use the photos primarily with my journal, I also really appreciate how thin the photo sheets are, so they don’t bulk up the pages too much. I truly enjoy printing out my little creations, cutting out my collages and then decorating my journal with them. 

I might not have my childhood back nor my Nirvana cassettes, but at least I’ve finally recaptured the joys of journaling — even if it did require a bit of help from a pocket printer.

title: Pixel Journal update rolls out Recorder integration, file export [U]
snippet: Following the last update in August, Google is rolling out a sizable update to Pixel Journal that adds Recorder audio entries and file exports. more…
fullText:
Following the last update in August, Google is rolling out a sizable update to Pixel Journal that adds Recorder audio entries and file exports.

Update 11/16: Updates for Pixel Journal (version 2026.10.27.x) and Pixel Recorder (4.2.20261001.x) are widely rolling out. After installing (be sure to open the apps and Force stop), you’ll see “Record new audio” and “Add existing recording” in the Add item menu. 

The first option directly launches the Recorder app into a new session, while the second brings up a list of previous recordings. The Journal app will show an inline audio player and transcript, which can be removed.

Curiously, these updates weren’t mentioned as part of the November 2026 Pixel Drop.

	

Journal November 2026 updates:

• Recorder integration: Record new audio or add existing recordings from Pixel Recorder, complete with playable clips and transcripts

• Journal export: Export your entries and media to view offline anytime

Original 11/10: From the “Add item” plus menu in entries, you’ll see “Record new audio” join the existing Take photo/video, Add photo, Health Connect activity, and location & map options.

At the moment, this audio integration is not live as Pixel Recorder also requires an update that we’re not seeing in the Play Store yet.

Being able to add a “voice entry with audio” is a pretty common feature for journaling apps. A transcription capability looks to be available for Google’s implementation.

Meanwhile, in Pixel Journal settings, there’s a new “Export your journal” option. This creates a ZIP file of all your entries, including images. Text is exported as HTML files. 

Version 2026.10.27.x of Pixel Journal is still rolling out via Google Play today.

title: You can now Email and Text (via Google Messages, iMessage) with Gemini
snippet: As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini. more…
fullText:
As previewed at I/O 2026, you can text — via Google Messages and iMessage — or email directly with Gemini.

Instead of using the Gemini app, you can now reach the AI assistant to “start tasks and get updates” using your preferred method of communication. To get started, go to gemini.google.com/channels.

You can now assign Gemini ‘tasks’ for free in six countries

Text with Gemini works via Google Messages and iMessage. Google does note that this method is “not end-to-end encrypted and may be accessible by your carrier.” The setup process involves verifying a phone number. Existing numbers associated with your Google Account appear automatically, and there’s the ability to add a new one. 

	

Afterward, you’ll receive a text from Gemini via RCS Business Messaging that offers a pretty straightforward chat experience. Before sending, booking, or other “major actions,” Gemini will ask for 1-tap confirmation.

…you can text a request, snap a photo of a school flyer to add dates to your Google Calendar, or get scheduled check-ins in a private 1:1 thread. If your plans change while Gemini is working, simply reply to the text to steer the task mid-run without starting over.

(Amusingly, Text with Gemini coexists with the existing Google Messages integration, which you can distinguish by the old blue/purple icon.)

Email with Gemini lets you “start tasks and get updates by emailing” gemini@google.com. Google explicitly names Gmail, Apple Mail, or Outlook as supported clients, while emails from Gemini are always “1:1 to you (never “Reply-All”) with a link to review and confirm your results.”

Forward a batch of school emails to add key dates to Google Calendar, spot schedule conflicts, or send over threads and PDFs to sort out medical bills and track insurance renewals. 

You can manage phone numbers and turn off both options from this new Channels page. If you’re more familiar with using your email client or phone’s messaging app, Text and Email with Gemini might boost your assistant usage. This is available first in the US.

Meanwhile, when announced in May, these two options were intended for Gemini Spark, which has since been integrated into the main Gemini experience as “tasks.”

title: You Can Now Fix Your Typos on Instagram Stories With an Edit Option
snippet: Instagram Stories can be edited for up to 15 minutes without losing engagement metrics.
fullText:
There are few things more anxiety-inducing than creating a well-crafted social media post and instantly finding it has a typo in it. Instagram Stories now lets you fix that.

Thanks to a recent update that includes several platform improvements, Instagram creators can edit their Stories up to 15 minutes after posting. You no longer have to start from scratch, and the edits won’t tank your engagement or sacrifice performance. To make changes to text, music, stickers, drawings or their placement or style, simply tap the menu at the bottom or the More button on your story to find the edit option. Instagram says that you won’t lose views, likes or replies as a result. After the 15-minute window closes, your Story can’t be changed without deleting it.

The edit option is a minor update but a welcome enhancement for those who regularly post on Instagram, said CNET’s Abrar Al-Heeti. It’s especially a plus if you always find something to nitpick after you set it live, she said. 

			

More from CNET

Al-Heeti also pointed to a recent update that lets you change a song on a published post. “It’s great to see Instagram adding more features that let you tweak something after it’s reached your audience, without losing out on any existing views or engagement.”

The Stories edit feature is slowly rolling out to all accounts, so first check whether your app is running the latest version.

In addition, Instagram is adding new stickers with a new sticker sheet, photo dumps that let you choose multiple pics more easily and new backgrounds including blur, colors and gradients. 

Earlier this week, Meta unveiled the Instagram-based chat app called Direct, which is currently in testing in Thailand and Turkey.

title: GTA 6 Launch Day Hits Different for Fired Rockstar Workers
snippet: Three people among the bigger group fired from Rockstar last year describe the “bittersweetness” of finally seeing the game they poured their hearts into out in the world.
fullText:
As people across the world sneak a day away from the office to play the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, the Rockstar employees who made the game are hopefully enjoying a well-earned day off in celebration. But not everyone who worked on the cultural juggernaut is joining the victory lap. 

For the 34 workers based in the UK and Canada who Rockstar dismissed in October 2025, GTA 6 launch day isn’t the day of celebration it should’ve been. 

“I should be with my team, taking a photo at every poster I can see, and be happy about it,” says Branimira Yordanova, who worked for three years in the lighting department at Rockstar North in Edinburgh, Scotland. “But it’s impossible because of how much hurt the firing has caused everyone.”

			

More from CNET

Rockstar fired the workers on the spot — something that’s only legal in the UK in cases of gross misconduct — alleging that they’d shared confidential company information on a Discord server.

The workers tell a different story. They say the company had long been aware of the Discord server, and only fired them when it started to look as though their efforts to unionize might succeed. They believe they were made an example of.

On the evening before the game’s launch, I spoke with Yordanova and her former colleague Dayne Oram, a senior production coordinator who had been at Rockstar North for seven years and was also affected by the dismissals, about how they were feeling about launch day. 

“One of our fellow colleagues said it the best,” says Yordanova. “What we’ll feel tomorrow is mourning what could have been, whether we want to or not.”

For all those who are mourning, others among the fired workers still hold a candle for GTA. Jacob Jones, who spent one year as a game tester before taking a role as a designer on the open world team for four years, was raring to play the game on launch day.

Jones graduated from being a childhood fan of the franchise – even counting the signatures of Rockstar co-founders Sam and Dan Hauser among his merch collection – to his dream job. He remains a GTA fan to this day, but describes feeling a sense of “poignance” and “bittersweetness” toward the launch.

Launching under a cloud

For Oram, Yordanova and Jones, GTA 6 eve was already a heavy day, even aside from the launch fever. 

They’re all part of a case brought by the Independent Workers’ Union of Great Britain on behalf of 23 former Rockstar North employees, who say they were unfairly dismissed for union activity. Hours before Oram and Yordanova spoke with me, a Glasgow employment tribunal had heard Rockstar’s closing submissions, which now leaves the fired workers in limbo as they wait for a verdict.

Rockstar North maintains that it fired the employees for gross misconduct. The company didn’t respond to a request for further comment.

Affected workers protesting outside the Glasgow Tribunal where their case is being heard.Andy Buchanan/AFP/Getty Images

Oram, Yordanova and Jones all speak highly of their former colleagues and teams, but Oram calls the sacking a “traumatic experience.” None have managed to secure alternative employment in the past 13 months. Jones says for now he’s focused on getting justice.

Meanwhile, reminders of their former employer have been everywhere as the studio geared up to release perhaps the most highly anticipated game of all time. Billboards, buses and online ads have been impossible to avoid, leaving Yordanova feeling “devastated.”

“I’ve genuinely had to make sure to avoid looking at it,” she says. “It’s such a cool game, and to know that you worked on it, you feel a sense of pride and joy to see it out. But it’s like that sense of joy has been taken away from us in such a ruthless manner.”

Oram acknowledges having “mixed feelings” about the launch. It’s been fantastic watching video footage of people playing and reviewing the game, they say. At the same time, they’ve found it difficult not being able to celebrate the moment with their former team.

Launch day plans

The workers fired from Rockstar North had varying ideas about whether they wanted to celebrate the launch, or avoid it entirely. Jones is one of those who started playing the game as soon as he got home from the tribunal at 1 a.m. By the time we spoke on Thursday, he’d played around six or seven hours.

“I personally think it’s a masterpiece,” he says. Even though he worked on the game, he’s discovering surprises everywhere. “I haven’t completed it yet, but I do think it is probably the greatest game ever made.”

Oram says that they planned to stick with watching streams of the game on launch day. “I’m probably not going to play the game for a little while, but I am looking forward to at least watching some people,” they say. Oram worked across so many bits of the game that there’s plenty they’re excited to see people discover.

Yordanova says she’s firmly in the avoidance camp. “I was really excited about playing the game in its official form because obviously when you work on it, you get to play it,” she says. “Even while we were in the office, there were parts I was really excited about – but I don’t think I’ll be playing it for the foreseeable future.”

She hopes that one day her feelings will change, she adds. “But right now, that’s just not possible in any way.”

The workers are currently awaiting a verdict from the judge.Lesley Martin/AFP/Getty Images

Instead, she’ll be spending the day with friends who supported her over the last year. She plans to “dive into another art form” by seeing the stop-motion animated film Wildwood at the cinema, which particularly appeals to her as a lighting artist.

Many people playing GTA 6 around the world won’t be aware of what happened to Oram, Yordanova, Jones and their colleagues during the game’s development, but the affected workers would like people to know. “I understand people just want to focus on the joy, but I don’t think you can separate the launch with what happened,” says Yordanova.

Reflecting on what happened, Jones says it’s such a shame the way things went down. “It was my absolute passion,” he says. “I just wish that the circumstances were different, and I would have loved to have still been there working on games. I wish I got to the end.”

				

					

						

													

					

					

						

Katie Collins
						

						

							Principal Writer						
					

											

								

											Katie is a UK-based news reporter and features writer. Officially, she is CNET's European correspondent, covering tech policy and Big Tech in the EU and UK. Unofficially, she serves as CNET's Taylor Swift correspondent. You can also find her writing about tech for good, ethics and human rights, the climate crisis, robots, travel and digital culture. She was once described a "living synth" by London's Evening Standard for having a microchip injected into her hand.

As people across the world sneak a day away from the office to play the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6 on Thursday, the Rockstar employees who made the game are hopefully enjoying a well-earned day off in celebration. But not everyone who worked on the cultural juggernaut is joining the victory lap.

For the 34 workers based in the UK and Canada who Rockstar dismissed in October 2025, GTA 6 launch day isn’t the day of celebration it should’ve been.

title: Epic accuses Apple of withholding 122,000 documents, seeks daily fines
snippet: In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details. more…
fullText:
In a new filing, Epic Games accuses Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to its proposed App Store commissions and asks the court to impose daily fines until the company complies. Here are the details.

A bit of background

As a result of the lawsuit Epic Games brought against Apple in 2020, Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers ruled in 2021 that Apple would have to, among other things, allow developers to direct users to alternative payment methods outside the App Store.

Apple responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them. This, in turn, led the court to find Apple in civil contempt for violating its injunction. Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn that ruling, a dispute that has now reached the Supreme Court.

At the same time, district court proceedings will determine what, if any, commission Apple may charge on purchases made through external payment links. Apple submitted its proposal on August 13, calling for commissions ranging from 5% to 15%, and Epic is expected to respond after Apple completes its document production.

In a new filing, however, Epic is accusing Apple of withholding more than 122,000 documents related to how it arrived at its proposed commission rates.

Epic’s new filing

One of the many aspects of the ever-sprawling battle between Epic Games and Apple centers on document production.

In its new filing, Epic says Apple has repeatedly failed to produce documents detailing how it arrived at its proposed commission rates, accusing the company of withholding materials it deems irrelevant to the proceedings.

Epic argues that Apple previously used questionable claims of attorney-client privilege to withhold documents during the contempt proceedings, but has now changed tactics.

From the filing:

Apple does introduce one tactical change from its prior campaign of delay. Whereas during the contempt proceeding Apple used bogus claims of privilege to evade its discovery obligations, this time Apple withholds thousands of documents on bogus claims of irrelevance. For example, Apple is withholding well over 99% of the documents returned by running the agreed-to search terms on the files of the four custodians Apple says decided on the proposed fee (Tim Cook, Eddy Cue, Carson Oliver, and Kevan Parekh (Apple’s new CFO)) and three other key individuals (Nate Barton, Alex Roman, and Phil Schiller). Apple claims these withheld documents are not relevant to this proceeding-even though they hit on case-specific terms such as “proffer,” “contempt,” “injunction,” and “link-out.” To put this into context, while Apple produced 632 custodial documents returned by these search terms (including families), Apple is withholding over 122,000 based on a claim of non-responsiveness. Moreover, Apple claims that it completed its production from the files of these custodians, yet its production does not include a single substantive email discussing the rates Apple ultimately proposed; any notes or communications reflecting what occurred at any meeting where these rates were discussed or decided; any internal analysis of the financial or business impact of the proposed commissions; any App Store profit and loss statements; or any support for Apple’s assertion that its incremental link-out costs are “essentially zero.”

Epic goes on to state that “Apple cannot be trusted to fix this problem on its own,” proposing instead that the court order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents matching the search terms agreed upon by both parties, regardless of whether Apple considers them relevant.

Under this proposal, Apple would still be allowed to review documents for attorney-client privilege, but it would be up to Epic to determine which of the remaining documents are relevant to the case. Epic argues that existing confidentiality protections would prevent it from using any of the information for purposes unrelated to the litigation.

From the filing:

Given Apple’s position, Epic respectfully submits that the Court should order Apple to produce to Epic all non-privileged documents that hit on the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms, so that Epic itself can sift the wheat from the chaff. Doing so will avoid further delays and place no burden on Apple. Moreover, doing so would not raise any of the concerns that required Special Master involvement in the prior proceeding, namely concerns around the production of privileged Apple information to Epic. Under Epic’s proposed remedy, Apple would be allowed to continue its review for privilege. For these reasons, Epic asks this Court to order Apple to produce all non-privileged documents that hit on any of the Parties’ agreed-upon search terms by December 2, 2026 (one week after Apple’s deadline to substantially complete production), irrespective of any relevance or responsiveness assessment.

Finally, though Epic does not propose a specific dollar amount, it “asks that the Court impose on Apple a daily monetary sanction for each day Apple fails to comply after December 2, 2026.”

According to the court docket, a hearing on Epic’s motion was initially scheduled for November 24 before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers. However, a new order filed today, which has yet to be made public, refers the discovery dispute to a magistrate judge and includes a notice terminating deadlines and hearings.

title: Review: Amazon’s Alexa Tablet 8 is a Fire Tablet with Google Play for $150 – what’s not to love?
snippet: Amazon shocked everyone in October when it launched its new Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets. For Black Friday 2026, the Alexa Tablet 8 is a mere $150 and, with Google Play on board, this feels like a Fire Tablet that’s all grown up. more…
fullText:
Amazon shocked everyone in October when it launched its new Alexa Tablet series with Google Play support built-in, addressing the biggest shortcoming of its older Fire Tablets. For Black Friday 2026, the Alexa Tablet 8 is a mere $150 and, with Google Play on board, this feels like a Fire Tablet that’s all grown up.

The Alexa Tablet 8 is one of three new Amazon tablets that launched in October with Google Play on board, and it’s also the one I was personally the most excited about. I love a good tiny Android tablet, but there just aren’t that many out there – and some of the ones we do have are exorbitantly expensive.

Right up there with Amazon’s long-running reputation in the tablet space, Alexa Tablet 8 is very much an affordable device, and that’s reflected in its fairly meager specs:

8.7-inch 1340×800 60Hz IPS LCD display

Android 16

MediaTek MT8189

4GB or 8GB of RAM

64GB or 128GB of storage (no microSD)

8MP rear camera / 5MP front camera

Yet, I didn’t find myself put off by the device.

	

I specifically asked Amazon for a review unit of the absolute base model – 4GB of RAM and lockscreen ads – and I can say with confidence it’s Not Bad at the end of the day.

The display is objectively not good, but it’s not really trying to be flashy either. The panel gets bright enough for most indoor use and, for general browsing or watching videos around the house or even on a flight, it gets the job done. If anything, my biggest complaint on the display was just how smudgey it gets with fingerprints.

Hardware is a strong suit. The Alexa Tablet 8 has an aluminum build that comes in this gorgeous teal color as well as a softer “Rosette” pink (or “Graphite,” if you want to keep it boring). It’s thin and light and slips into a bag easily, and even fit into the back pocket of my jeans. Buttons are clicky and aspects such as the speakers actually do well enough – like the display, the speakers aren’t good, but they’re not bad by any stretch either.

Amazon has a folio cover available that’s simple but nice, with a fabric finish that’s grippy. It’s an extra $40, though, which feels like a bit much for a super-affordable Android slate.

The biggest question was around the software experience, and this is where this new effort really shines.

Alexa Tablet 8 ships with Android 16 out of the box, not FireOS or whatever Amazon was calling its forked experience on Fire Tablets (I genuinely refuse to go double-check because it’s a memory I’m thrilled to never have to revisit). It’s a pretty “stock” experience, with Amazon leaving aspects such as the notification shade/quick settings alone, and even the Settings menu feels pretty clean. 

That’s not to say nothing has changed. The homescreen has a fairly standard layout , but with these neat little corner widgets – one a “dynamic” widget with scrolling content (mostly ads) and the other a shortcut for Alexa search. Amazon is pushing Alexa as a voice assistant pretty heavily on these tablets, but I’m happy to report it’s pretty easy to ignore if you choose. These tablets will be great additions to your Alexa ecosystem if you’re invested, but I’m simply not.

The biggest change you’ll find is the lockscreen, where Amazon’s base models all come with lockscreen ads. This saves you about $20 on the hardware, and it’s not that bad of an experience. That said, I’d absolutely spend the extra $20 at purchase to go without them, especially seeing as this blocks the ability to set a lockscreen wallpaper at all. It doesn’t cost anything more to remove them later, though, with a $20 charge through your Amazon account removing ads.

But what’s important here is that, for the fire time, Amazon is admitting defeat and installing the Google Play Store.

Alexa Tablet 8, and the rest of the lineup, has Google Play out of the box and access to any app you want. This means that you can, if you choose, fully ignore Amazon’s own services and do whatever you want. The smallest of examples: While Amazon’s built-in keyboard is fine, it’s wonderful that I don’t have to jump through hoops to switch over to Gboard. Fire Tablets were always an enticing value with a big catch, but Amazon’s change in this regard truly makes Alexa Tablets an attractive option for everyone – not just those willing to put up with the restriction or put in the work to hack Google apps on board.

Performance, despite the meager specs, is not awful. MediaTek’s low-end chip has just enough horsepower for general use, and 4GB of RAM isn’t as detrimental as I would have expected. It’s not fast by any means, but you could do a lot worse. There are 4GB Android tablets I’ve literally decided not to review because I couldn’t use them past the setup process, so the fact that Amazon is delivering a completely usable experience is a win in my book, even more so that I don’t actually mind using it. There’s a caveat to that, of course, and it’s that you shouldn’t expect to do a ton on this base model. For light browsing, reading Kindle books (or whatever other reading app since, you know, Google Play), or watching videos, this is great. For games, you’ll want to look elsewhere (and expect to spend more). 

“Not awful” is kind of the pattern here. 

Alexa Tablet 8 isn’t some shining example of a perfect budget tablet, but I think it really nails the fundamentals. At its usual $230~ starting price, it’s a plenty-good deal for those in the market for an affordable Android slate, but the Black Friday pricing of just $150 is all the better – I just wish the model with 8GB of RAM was also on sale.

Alexa Tablet 8 at Amazon – Starting at $149.99 for Black Friday

Amazon’s pivot to Alexa Tablets is great – though I hope the company knows full well that everyone is still going to call these Fire Tablets or Kindles or whatever combination of brands that spring to mind. But that reputation might work in Amazon’s favor at the end of the day. While there’s a huge portion of the audience that’s been left frustrated for years at the lack of Play Store support on Fire Tablets, they’ve still been a market success for the most part, so this shift is just a win for everyone. Users get a better experience, Amazon gets to shuffle its priorities away from a dead app store, and the market as a whole gets an affordable piece of hardware that doesn’t suck.

What’s not to love?

					

Amazon’s new Alexa Tablet 8 ushers in a new era after Fire Tablet with the Play Store in tow, and it’s a win for everyone involved, including the customer.

					

				

Pros

				

											

Affordable prices + Play Store – what's not to love?

											

Polished and fun hardware

											

Good enough performance despite meager specs

									

			

					

				

Cons

				

											

Display, speakers, and performance are objectively not great

											

Lockscreen ads on base models

title: Fitbit Edge after 30 days: Life in the middle lane [Video]
snippet: The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included. more…
fullText:
The biggest compliment you can pay Google at the moment is that alongside the Pixel Watch, recent Fitbit releases have been a huge return to form – the Fitbit Edge included.

I need to nail my colors to the mast; I’m a Fitbit Air fanboy. I’ve talked about it multiple times on the Pixelated podcast, here on the site, and it made me switch away from the Pixel Watch 5 because of how easily it fit into my existence without insisting on itself.

Fitbit Edge Review: Too much and too little at the same time

The Fitbit Edge worried me at first because it comes with a screen, which is something I realized isn’t that important to me day-to-day. After 30 days of wear, I’m conflicted because maybe I was too hasty to ditch a display on my wrist.

For more video content, subscribe to 9to5Google on YouTube.

	

More but simultaneously less

The design is somewhat in a halfway house because it feels like it’s trying to be both a classic Fitbit while integrating some of the Pixel Watch features we know and love. Initially, I loved it, but it has become something that isn’t quite enough in either direction to suit my own tastes.

My love for the simplicity of the Fitbit Air has colored how I feel, but the Edge has an excellent core design. The display bezels remind me heavily of the original Pixel Watch; yes, they’re there, but you only notice them when the light catches the frame edge.

After a month of daily wear, the display has lost a bit of its luster. The oleophobic coating is just about holding up, but now we’re into the cooler months; it’ll be put through a barrage of jacket cuffs and hoodie sleeves. This is one of the only durability concerns I have had so far.

Despite that admittedly minor concern, the Fitbit Edge is not something you need to baby. I’ve bashed it with weights, caught my wrist on zips (zippers for you, my American friends), and bashed it around with reckless abandon. It’s solid and hasn’t picked up as much as a single scuff. I don’t care too much if a fitness tracker gets a beating, whereas I would be more concerned about damaging my Pixel Watch.

What it’s like to use

If you come in wanting a smartwatch-like experience from the Fitbit Edge, I think you’ll instantly be frustrated by the UI. It can feel cramped when you see notifications, and the large bezels don’t help all that much, but Google has well optimized almost all of the key sections outside of this.

Tiles are very well implemented; they’re just a smaller, squatter take on the Pixel Watch tile system, and it’s one of the best things about the Fitbit Edge interface. It’s also really snappy, which is something that isn’t the case with cheaper fitness trackers such as this. I’m constantly checking the weather or using the Google Health tile, but I have loved the quick access complication on the default watch face.

I tried a few of the other designs over the past 30 days; a lot of them are great. The default has become my favorite. It’s information-dense without being too overloaded. Tapping the complications takes you to the exact data point. I genuinely love how fuss-free an experience it is, save for a few minor complaints.

We could criticize the accuracy of the data or the lack of tracking for certain types of workouts, but I think that misses the point of the Fitbit Edge. It’s a simple tracker with a screen, and the fact that you get even basic ECG on a device of this size is impressive.

I truly have worn the Edge daily for a full month, and while the bands are comfortable, I have found that they cause me to get a rash on the underside of my left wrist just under the palm. It’s actively stopping me from wearing it all the time now. I hope that the new connector doesn’t slow down third-party development for bands, because I’m desperate for a fabric band to alleviate this issue.

This is exacerbated when the rubber band gets wet or sweaty. If you have sensitive skin, you might have the same problem as I have. Using some moisturizer has helped, but it is something I wasn’t prepared to suffer with before the Fitbit Edge turned up. I get that this is likely a “me” problem, but I wanted to note it.

When the screen gets wet or moist, it can bug out quite a lot. Taps don’t register properly, and a few water droplets can activate all the menus and submenus. Luckily, it won’t force your phone to place a call or anything like that, but the water protection mode is a must. I have kept it on extensively.

Swimmers will probably get super frustrated; heck, I was on a rainy day as the screen kept bugging out. Overall, though, I have enjoyed the fitness tracking. Unlike on the Fitbit Air, it is nice to have a screen to start a workout rather than head over to my phone. That said, the experience is the same as on your phone, but scaled down to fit the watch face.

I dislike that you don’t get a phone notification to show the current workout progress by default, like the Fitbit Air. I had become accustomed to that. Luckily, you can enable it in the Google Health settings. I like having this as I forget to stop workouts so often without a prompt to hit “stop.”

With audio playback, you’re also getting the partial benefits of watch-phone controls, but it’s a two-step process unlike on Pixel Watch. You either have to go to the “Media” app or have the tile active and navigate to it to access play/pause and all your other streaming app controls. I tend not to bother using these as it’s finicky.

This had me thinking about NFC. I think a lot of people would have liked NFC for Google Wallet on the Fitbit Edge, but I think having to enter a PIN on such a small screen would really have been a nightmare. I’ve made wireless payments with my watch less than five times, as it’s just easier to use my phone rather than contort my wrist to a wireless payment terminal. I figure this was something that was thought about and makes a lot of sense given the constraints.

One of my other complaints is that the DND and Bedtime modes from my account haven’t synced or at least don’t appear to sync. Unless I’m mistaken, you need to activate these settings manually every time, which has been super annoying when in bed, as a flick of your wrist can blind you in a dark room. I figure this is something that can be fixed with an update, so here’s hoping.

I’ve been super impressed with the battery life. A week is easily attainable for me with up to three gym visits per week, so I’ve charged 5 times in a month. That, to me, is excellent. I picked up a cheap charging dock, as the Edge uses the same charger for the Fitbit Air, so I figured why not.

It’s not the best-looking dock, but I quite like how it airs off my Edge so it’s not as stinky after gym sessions – as I wipe with an alcohol pad and clean as regularly as possible.

Who is this for?

The experience is fine; it’s almost a third of the price of the Pixel Watch and lacks a few features due to the various compromises – compromises I can deal with, as smartwatches have become information overload for me over time, and I like that the app selection is ultra-refined. At no point does the Fitbit Edge give you information overload.

Coming from a Charge 6 or an older Fitbit, this is an amazing replacement. It’s the new “default” fitness tracker for people who want all the hallmarks of what makes a great Fitbit.

There is just enough. Nothing more, nothing less. To me, this feels like the perfect middle ground for a lot of people. You want something simple, touchscreen-enabled, and that doesn’t get in the way. As impressed as I have been with the Edge, though, I’ve loved a fuss-free tech accessory so much recently that I’ll probably go back to the Fitbit Air.

title: Andrey Zvyagintsev believes filmmakers know what the audience wants — not executives

fullText:
The year is 2022. Vladimir Putin has announced the military draft. In Andrey Zvyagintsev’s Minotaur, set in the fictional town of Krasoborsk, a quietly unhappy couple, called Gleb and Galina, carry on with their lives, or try to, geopolitics notwithstanding. For Galina, carrying on means an affair, which we deduce from a scene of her texting with a faint smile, her face lit in the dark by the light of her phone. (Minotaur is a remake of Claude Chabrol’s 1969 film The Unfaithful Wife, whose title gives the plot away more readily than Zvyagintsev’s.)

Meanwhile, Gleb runs a kind of private contracting concern and is soon asked to scare up military recruits to meet a quota. At this point, the domestic noir and the workplace drama merge to dramatic, devastating, and darkly funny effects.

In Minotaur, as in his five other features, Zvyagintsev has the camera moving seemingly objectively, almost omnisciently, putting the characters in their context. Occasionally they appear rather small, especially when set against the epic scale of their mythic and biblical fates. That the environment shapes the person seems to be a recurring revelation across all six of his staggering films. Minotaur, too, opens with a natural landscape of the arboreal kind and ends with another, different landscape, of clouds. In the middle is a movie about people trying to make sense of the landscapes they find themselves in, of the social, moral, relational variety.

Zvyagintsev has some experience with finding oneself in incomprehensible landscapes. After receiving Russia’s Sputnik V covid-19 vaccine during the pandemic, he fell ill, and later learned about the invasion of Ukraine while recovering from a medical coma in Germany. He subsequently chose not to return home, moving to France.

At the Cannes Film Festival in May, Minotaur won the second-highest honor. In his acceptance speech, Zvyagintsev spoke about the war, saying: “The only person who can stop this butchery is the President of the Russian Federation. Put an end to this carnage. The whole world is waiting for it.” While he resists the identity of exile, in September the Russian government designated him a “foreign agent.”

Minotaur is based on Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife.

Zvyagintsev returned this year to the New York Film Festival, where he last visited with his 2014 film Leviathan, which won a Golden Globe and was nominated for an Oscar. His debut in 2003, The Return, won a top prize at Venice International Film Festival, after which he was invited to meet Putin, an account of which appears in his forthcoming book. Out of his six films, four have won prestigious prizes at Cannes, including Elena and Loveless.

We discussed the three years he spent cleaning the streets of Moscow in the early 1990s, his status as a Russian immigrant in France now, and how he captures that great Chekhovian instinct: that life is wretched, but what can we do, we must go on living. Zvyagintsev spoke to The Verge through a translator from Los Angeles.

I understand you went from cleaning streets to making commercials. What happened in between?

It kind of happened almost at the same time, because I was cleaning the streets to be able to live in Moscow. From 1990 to 1993, I was cleaning the streets. And then I was going to the Museum of Cinema and watching a movie every single day. Those were my formative years, when I learned a lot about cinema.

And then I was let go.

I had been living in a huge communal flat, free accommodation in a beautiful historic mansion in central Moscow. It was a really big apartment, and there were three street cleaners, including me, that lived there. In 1993, I was forced to leave the apartment after someone from the local housing administration decided to take it over. The two others had families, so they decided that if someone was supposed to move, it was going to be me, since I was single.

I was offered alternative accommodation, but realized that the only reason I had continued working as a street sweeper was to keep that particular apartment.

So the first night when I had to leave the apartment, I left it fast without an actual plan. I had to spend the night inside a truck that was abandoned and that was parked in the street.

I got a new job as a guard, as a night guard at a kindergarten where I also ate leftover food from the children’s meals.

After the first day, I called my friend who was working in commercials and doing music videos. I asked him to help with a job, because I was sure I was able to shoot commercials. After the first commercial, I met some producers who liked my work, and then I started shooting commercials on the regular and working as a freelance for some time. One of those commercials was noticed by a producer from a TV channel called REN TV, who was shooting a bunch of TV series at the time. His name was Dmitry Lesnevsky and he asked me whether I wanted to shoot movies, and I said it was my dream. And then Dmitry presented me with 15 scripts of choice, and I shot three episodes of a television series called The Black Room for this channel, each 25 minutes long.

How did you know this friend?

We were army friends. He was a close friend from the army. He was a cinema mechanic. He was starting movies for the soldiers when they were in the army. They had a theater, and I was in the music ensemble in the army. He was also an actor.

You had an adverse reaction to a covid vaccine. You were ill for a long time. You nearly died. You moved, and eventually settled in France. You’ve said you can’t know how that experience changed you as a filmmaker, but I’m curious if you know how that experience changed you as a person.

I got sick in Russia. I was in a coma for 40 days in Germany. I had a major problem with my lungs, a bacteria called klebsiella found its way there. They thought that they would need a lung transplant. Fortunately, the Germans were able to operate, and the transplant was not needed. I moved to France a year later after the coma.

What was the biggest change for me was the rhythm of life. I understood that you cannot lose time, so I’m trying to do things in a much more dynamic manner, and not leave things for later because we don’t know if this later exists. So that that’s the biggest change, really, just seeing life as something that passes by quickly.

You are a vocal opponent of the current Russian government. Do you consider yourself to be in political exile?

I am not in political exile. I did not have that status, and I never applied for it because I don’t see any necessity for that. I consider myself an immigrant. I’ve been living away from my native country for almost five years, but I did not leave on purpose. I was already in Europe when the war happened. There is a term in Russian, called nevozvrashchenets, which means a person who does not come back, someone who has left their home country and has not returned, particularly for political reasons. I was in the clinic in Germany and then in France when the war started, and I realized that I could not go back to the country that is at war.

You’ve said you are not political, but your movies seem overtly political, to me. You’ve also said that the job of an artist is to reflect reality. You don’t think you’re political, but your job is to reflect reality, and we are living at a time when politics is dominant. How do you reconcile all this?

It’s very simple to reconcile. It’s just that the politics barges into our lives, and we have to reflect what’s going on in the world. You become a witness of what’s going on beyond your window, what’s going on to the environment, to the world around you, to the world close to you. It just so happens that the politics dominate our lives. We are witnessing historical events that we cannot not reflect in the movies.

“There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews… This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power”

When I say I’m not a political animal, I mean that I have no way of influencing the political process in my country, especially while the war is going on. There is no politics in Russia, in the sense of politics being a struggle for power, dialogue between different parties or worldviews, you know, left, right, Democrats, Republicans. This does not exist in Russia. There’s only one power.

It feels more like domination in the way Foucault meant it.

Yes. It’s not even that there is only one party that dominates. It’s that no one even questions it, and no one even tries to struggle. It’s kind of a totalitarian regime at this time.

Let’s talk Minotaur. I believe you said you wanted to adapt Ingrid Bergman first, but when that didn’t go, you asked your producers for other available properties and they sent you a list. You also said you asked for marital dramas from the ’60s and ’70s specifically. Why?

I wanted to do a remake of a movie that would have three or four main characters, not a lot of different locations, that would be a little more compact, because there was a certain budget consideration. The films that I had previously considered, the scripts I considered, were more expensive, and so I was not able to get any of them going.

And that’s when I asked for the list from my friend who is French, and he gave me a list of French films. If I had an Italian friend, those would have been Italian movies.

I asked him for the best films from the ’60s and ’70s because it’s far away enough for us, those were probably the films that were a little bit more forgotten by the public, or a new generation of the public maybe hasn’t seen them. And that’s how I discovered Claude Chabrol’s The Unfaithful Wife.

You also said that something about the Chabrol did not work for you, and that’s what gave you the inspiration to want to remake it.

I wouldn’t formulate it as something not working, but I would rather say that he made a kind of a formal choice when it comes to the office life of the main character. Chabrol concentrates more on the crime plot and the love triangle [than the office life], which is totally his right.

And I thought it was something that I would like to fill in. In 2022, the war was going on, and then in September they started the partial mobilization in Russia, and so this plot kind of just barged into our movie, and filled out that space that was empty previously.

Your movies are full of scenes Hollywood executives would ask to cut. I am thinking of the ending of Minotaur, with the clouds, or The Banishment, which ends with women collecting hay and they are singing. What is the effect of these moments in your movies?

It would be impossible to cut out those moments.

What are they doing in the movie?

When you say that Hollywood execs would probably like to cut that stuff out, the viewers, including viewers in Hollywood, really like the clouds [that Minotaur ends on], for example, and they even tell me that the sequence could have been longer. So I want to tell you that the execs do not know what the viewers want because when the viewer goes to the cinema, he kind of goes to sleep and then he watches a dream. And as long as this dream is aesthetically pleasing and harmonious and beautiful, that’s what the viewers should be watching, and no one should cut that out.

This is the key conflict between the producer and the creator. The producer does not trust the creator to know what the audience wants, but the creator knows. And so, if the producer is so sure of himself, he should write a script himself.

You published a book about the making of your third film, Elena. I understand you’re working on a second book. What can you tell us about this project? Will it include advice to young filmmakers?

The whole book, in a way, will be an advice to younger filmmakers, or people who love movies, because it will be a very detailed account of the six films that I have released so far, six conversations with one of the best cinema critics writing in Russian, Anton Dolin.

Would you ever work in another language apart from Russian or with Netflix?

Yes, I am open. In fact, I have a script in English. Two even.

title: UN court cites military Facebook posts while finding Myanmar guilty of genocide
snippet: Rohingya refugees in Bangladesh watch the International Court of Justice’s ruling on Myanmar’s genocide against its Muslim minority. | Photo by Salahuddin Ahmed / AFP via Getty Images In its ruling that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya people in 2016 and 2017, the United Nations' top court says that Facebook played a role in helping Myanmar's military spread hate speech against its Muslim minority. fullText:
Emma Roth

 

is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

In its ruling that Myanmar committed state-sponsored genocide against the Rohingya people in 2016 and 2017, the United Nations’ top court says that Facebook played a role in helping Myanmar’s military spread hate speech against its Muslim minority. The ruling from the International Court of Justice determined that Facebook posts made by the country’s military “dehumanized” the Muslim minority “and at times encouraged and legitimized violence against them,” as reported earlier by Reuters.

The decision that Myanmar committed genocide comes after The Gambia sued the country in 2019 over the military’s violent “clearance operations” targeting the Rohingya Muslims. The military relied heavily on Facebook, which was the most popular platform in Myanmar at the time of the attacks, with a 2022 report from Amnesty International finding that the platform “proactively amplified and promoted content on the Facebook platform which incited violence, hatred, and discrimination against the Rohingya.” Despite numerous warnings from human rights activists, Amnesty International said Facebook failed to stop the spread of hateful content in Myanmar.

The UN is now backing up these findings. It cites a report from the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), which says that a post made by the military ahead of its August 25th, 2017 massacres on the Rohingya people “unleashed a torrent of public vitriol,” with over 200 comments calling for Rohingya people “to be shot, killed, exterminated or permanently removed from Myanmar.”

Facebook later removed military-linked pages containing thousands of posts with anti-Rohingya hate speech published between July and December 2017, according to the IIMM. The company admitted in 2018 that it didn’t do enough to prevent the incitement of violence in Myanmar, and later introduced a “corporate human rights policy” that includes an annual report about its impact on human rights. The Verge reached out to Meta with a request for comment but didn’t immediately hear back.

Group Chat

The game is finally here, and there’s plenty to discuss.

by  Andrew Webster

Nov 20, 2026, 3:00 PM UTC

Image: Cath Virginia / The Verge, Rockstar

Andrew Webster

 

is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.

It’s hard to believe, but Grand Theft Auto VI is now a real thing that we all can play. Thirteen years after GTA V, and eight years since Red Dead Redemption 2, Rockstar is back with its latest sprawling, extravagant open world. There’s a lot to experience — and a lot to talk about.

Perhaps the most impressive thing about GTA VI is how flexible it is, letting you mold the experience to your own play style. You can still be a maniacal criminal, but you can also focus on the new love story that includes an entire button dedicated to holding hands. Or you can spend the hours fishing or driving around listening to the radio. Maybe you just want to doomscroll through a fake version of Instagram. As GTA VI producer Rob Nelson told me just ahead of launch, “It’s a risk. It’s a real change for Grand Theft Auto. You can still play it the old way, you can reject all of this stuff. But for people who do engage, it’s meaningful — you’re earning it, you’re working at it, just like in a normal relationship.”

Now that the game is out and people are finding their own way through Leonida, it’s a great time to start talking about it. I’ve played through the entire main story — you can read my review right here — but I’m nowhere close to experiencing everything in the game. But I’m happy to answer any questions you have, though I’ll be careful around some of the big story spoilers. I’ll also be joined by senior reporter Jay Peters, who is still early in the game and can offer a different perspective. There’s a good chance some other Verge staff will stop by as well, since we’re basically all playing it.

So drop all of your questions, theories, and stray thoughts about GTA VI here. I’ll be checking in throughout the day to join the conversation in the comments.

title: Gemini skills add file support and sharing ahead of Gems deprecation
snippet: Ahead of the Gems shutdown that starts rolling out tomorrow, Google is adding two key features to Gemini skills. more…
fullText:
Ahead of the Gems shutdown that starts rolling out tomorrow, Google is adding two key features to Gemini skills.

These “reusable, custom instructions” now support files from your device, Google Drive, Gemini Notebook, and Google Photos that can be used as context. You can upload files, up to 100 MB, when you create a skill.

Gemini will “reference these files every time the skill runs in chats and tasks.” Files from Drive and Notebooks will “update in real time so your skill always works from the latest version.” 

Meanwhile, skills can now be shared. Go to the Gemini app’s Customize > Skills page on the web to grant View or Edit permissions. Recipients will receive an email and can review the skill before adding it.

	

Use cases for these new capabilities include:

A marketing team can share a brand-voice skill that references their brand guidelines doc in Drive.

A team lead can share an onboarding skill grounded in the team handbook.

A teacher can share a lesson-planning skill built on a notebook containing their curriculum.

File support and sharing for Gemini skills are rolling out over the coming weeks for everyone: “Available to all Google Workspace customers and users with personal Google accounts.”

title: Alleged Pixel 11 Pro prototype had HiLight and a temperature sensor
snippet: Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype shows off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the new HiLight LED in one. more…
fullText:
Google might have had a chance to keep the temperature sensor around, it seems, as a supposed prototype shows off a device that offered both the last-gen temperature sensor and the new HiLight LED in one.

Images posted to Telegram (via NotebookCheck) show an apparent prototype of the Pixel 11 Pro XL. The device is seen with the markings that are common to other known Pixel prototypes, with the key difference compared to the final model being the fact that the camera bar has both a temperature sensor and HiLight.

We can tell this is HiLight due to the diffused rear LED, and we know this isn’t a Pixel 10 Pro XL because the camera bar has full-width glass instead of a metal portion.

Google pulled the plug on the temperature sensor in Pixel 11 Pro after the prior three generations offered the feature. While the sensor was never particularly beloved, Google did see backlash from the lack of functionality in HiLight at launch. Having both features may have resulted in a different sentiment around the updated hardware.

title: Disney+ and Hulu’s ‘fully unified’ app is coming next month
snippet: Disney has announced a major milestone coming next month in its plans to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon. more…
fullText:
Disney has announced a major milestone coming next month in its plans to merge the Disney+ and Hulu apps, which will be “fully unified” into Disney+ soon.

Disney+ app will fully integrate all Hulu features starting in December

Today Disney reported its quarterly earnings and gave an update on plans to merge Disney+ and Hulu into one app.

Here’s what the company said:

Our app unification of Disney+ and Hulu is nearly complete. Beginning this December, subscribers will have a fully unified experience on Disney+, including live TV and select premium add-ons, creating a more seamless way to discover and engage with the breadth of content across our brands and franchises.

Live TV and premium add-ons were the final Hulu features that hadn’t yet been imported to the Disney+ app. But by adding those capabilities into Disney+, the app unification will be “complete.”

	

Disney hasn’t said how quickly the Hulu app will be discontinued. But it likely won’t happen until sometime in 2027 at the earliest. The company will want to provide abundant transition time and not risk upsetting its paying subscribers.

The ultimate goal of unifying everything in Disney+, though, will be accomplished soon.

Also in the earnings report, Disney said that creator content will start appearing in the Disney+ app in December. This is related to the company’s deal with TikTok that debuted after its previous OpenAI deal fell apart when Sora was killed off. The Disney+ app will also get “more vertical video, live sports, and podcasts” soon too, Disney said.

title: iPhone Duo gets one of Face ID’s best features with upcoming iOS 27.3 update
snippet: Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo. more…
fullText:
Soon, your alarms, timers, and phone calls will be less disruptive on iPhone Duo.

Unlock with Front Camera feature 

With today’s iOS 27.3 developer beta 2, iPhone Duo gained a new feature: Unlock with Front Camera. This lets you unlock your iPhone Duo in a similar fashion to Face ID, but using the front selfie camera, rather than Face ID’s TrueDepth 3D camera system. But, Face ID is more than just unlocking: it also provides Attention Aware features.

Attention Aware features come to iPhone Duo

Attention Aware features, which were first introduced with iPhone X, check for when you’re looking at the phone before performing certain actions:

iPhone will check for attention before dimming the display, expanding a notification when locked, or lowering the volume of some alerts.

Previously, Attention Aware features required Face ID, but iOS 27.3 extends it to iPhone Duo. Like the new face unlock feature, Attention Aware features only work when using the outer display. However, the face unlock feature does not have to be set up to use the Attention Aware features.

After updating to iOS 27.3, the features should be automatically enabled. You can enable or disable the feature in Settings → Accessibility → Face Recognition & Attention. You can also enable Haptic on Successful Unlock there, just like an iPhone with Face ID.

In my experience, Attention Aware features will lower the volume of alarms, timers, and incoming calls when your iPhone is already unlocked. It also will prevent the display from dimming and locking while you are actively looking at it. Finally, it will expand and show notification content on the Lock Screen after unlocking with the new face unlock feature.

title: Are the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro the best earbuds for you?
snippet: Picking the right earbuds is a tough task, but Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are among the best on the market, and in this guide, we’ll be looking at whether or not they’re the best earbuds for you this holiday season. more…
fullText:
Picking the right earbuds is a tough task, but Samsung’s Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are among the best on the market, and in this guide, we’ll be looking at whether or not they’re the best earbuds for you this holiday season.

This post is sponsored by Samsung

Do Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound good?

In short, yes, the Galaxy Buds 4 Pro sound great. Samsung’s flagship earbuds have a balanced sound profile that’s customizable by the listener to suit their tastes, and is generally recognized as having excellent sound quality by experts and owners alike.

Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are award-winning earbuds with balanced sound quality for music lovers, offering a clean and crisp profile that lets you hear music the way you’ll enjoy it most.

	

Samsung’s flagship earbuds deliver their sound through a new, larger main driver that’s paired with a dedicated tweeter. They support 24-bit/96 kHz UHQ audio when paired with a compatible Samsung Galaxy device. That’s paired with active noise cancellation that adjust to your surroundings in real-time. They also sound good for those on the other end of a call, with Samsung’s Super Clear Call tech reducing noise from your environment, and the blade stem design positioning the microphones closer to your mouth.

What features are on Galaxy Buds 4 Pro?

Like everything else in Samsung’s product lineup, Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are packed with useful features.

This includes active noise cancellation (ANC) to filter out noise in your surroundings. Samsung even adapts ANC strength to what’s around you, raising the ANC level when you’re somewhere like on a plane, but lowering it when you’re in a quiet park or café. Voice and Siren Detect can automatically switch the earbuds to Ambient mode when you begin a conversation or when an emergency siren is detected.

Live Translate offers support for 22 languages to help you have a conversation beyond the language barrier, with speech translated into your ears via Buds 4 Pro and the transcript shown on your phone. Bixby and Gemini are accessible through the earbuds for AI assistance, too. Samsung also offers an FDA-approved hearing aid feature to help amplify sounds around you. 

Head gestures allow you to answer or decline calls with a simple shake of your head. Pinch controls manage playback, while swiping adjusts the volume; pinch-and-hold can be customized for supported shortcuts.

Do I have to use Galaxy Buds 4 Pro with a Samsung phone?

No, you don’t have to have a Samsung Galaxy smartphone to use Galaxy Buds 4 Pro.

Because they work over standard Bluetooth, Samsung’s best earbuds work with any smartphone, tablet, and other devices. Galaxy Buds 4 Pro can also connect to Windows PCs as standard Bluetooth audio, although advanced features are more limited outside the Galaxy ecosystem.

That said, you’ll get the best experience with Samsung devices. That’s in part because EQ, noise cancellation, and other controls are baked into One UI, but also because Samsung’s best audio codec on Galaxy Buds 4 Pro is proprietary to Galaxy devices. In other words, you’ll get the best sound quality on these earbuds when paired to another Samsung device.

Can I get a good deal on Galaxy Buds 4 Pro?

Galaxy Buds 4 Pro are typically sold for $249.99, but it’s not hard to find a good deal, especially during the holiday season. Best Buy is going to be one of the best resources here, with discounts available throughout the holiday season alongside convenient in-store pickup.
