title: Why iPhone Duo wasn’t for me (but might be for you)
snippet: I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you. more…
fullText:
I’ve had the iPhone Duo for nearly two weeks now, and have officially decided to return it. Here are the three main reasons why the Duo didn’t work out for me, but might for you.

#1: One-handed use is my default

I use my iPhone one-handed all the time, and based on my experience, iPhone Duo is clearly intended to be used with two hands. You can use it one-handed, but for me it’s not nearly as comfortable as the iPhone 18 Pro. It’s too wide and too heavy to be used for long.

Perhaps over time I’d get used to needing two hands for most iPhone interactions. But that would be a pretty significant shift for me, as there are so many situations when I don’t have both hands free.

If you already use two hands with your iPhone regularly—perhaps because you have a Pro Max model—then the Duo’s one-handed experience likely won’t bother you. But the more I used the Duo, the more I found myself missing my iPhone 18 Pro.

#2: The inner display didn’t draw me in

The biggest value proposition of a foldable is that it’s a 2-in-1 product, letting you have a standard phone but also a tablet-sized display that fits in your pocket.

I totally get the appeal, and fully expected to love that hybrid design. But after two weeks of trying, I still struggled to find times when I actually wanted to unfold the Duo. And to be clear, that’s a me problem, not an issue with the Duo itself.

I tried a bunch of apps on the inner display, and struggled to find use cases that—for me—made it worthwhile to open the Duo. But based on the feedback I’ve seen from most Duo owners, I’m very much in the minority.

I know lots of people love the Duo for video, but I don’t watch much video on my iPhone. I almost never watch YouTube, TikTok, or Instagram Reels. And for shows and movies, I stick with my TV screen and an Apple TV 4K.

Multitasking support on iPhone Duo works really well. But when I found myself needing to multitask, I still reached for my iPad Pro with Magic Keyboard attached. A keyboard-free product can’t replace my main computer (nor would I expect it to), and the Duo screen was too small to comfortably work on it.

#3: I want the best camera system

Last year I bought an iPhone Air and absolutely loved it. Initially, the Air’s less capable camera system didn’t bother me, it was “good enough.”

After a few months though, I started missing the Pro camera system more. Then I learned that my wife was pregnant with twins, and I knew I wanted the best possible iPhone cameras to capture their early weeks and months. So I bought an iPhone 18 Pro in September.

I’ve been very impressed by iPhone 18 Pro’s Main camera upgrades, and it’s great having a Telephoto lens again too. Since having the best camera system is so crucial for me right now, I knew iPhone Duo couldn’t be my only iPhone.

I initially planned to dual-carry the two models, using iPhone 18 Pro solely as a camera. But over and over I found myself wishing it was my only iPhone.

	

Is the iPhone Duo camera good enough for most people? Probably so. But for this year at least, with my twins aging rapidly, it’s not quite right for me. If I loved the Duo for other reasons, I would just use both models. But since I didn’t, I’m happy to stick with the iPhone 18 Pro.

iPhone Duo wrap-up: This is not a bad review

In closing, I want to explicitly state that I don’t think the iPhone Duo is a bad product, and this isn’t a “bad review.”

The iPhone Duo just isn’t for me. I get the sense, though, that it’s lots of people’s favorite iPhone in years. Apple created its most unique new iPhone model since the original, and there’s plenty to love about it. I’m very curious to see how popular foldables become over time compared to slab models, because each clearly offers pros and cons. But for me, at least right now, the iPhone 18 Pro is my model of choice.

What has your iPhone Duo experience been like so far? Love it? Undecided? Let us know in the comments.

title: Google Voice app gets a redesign on Android, and it screams RCS [Gallery]
snippet: Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a big neon sign that says “RCS is coming.” more…
fullText:
Google Voice is a wonderful service that’s often neglected, but with RCS supposedly on the way, a new app redesign is now rolling out on Android that might as well have a big neon sign that says “RCS is coming.”

Google Voice is a US-only service that operates a phone number over the internet. No normal carrier, just an app tied to your Google account that gets a phone number with the ability to make calls and send/receive text messages. The latter, though, has been a point of contention for the past few years as Voice was excluded from Google’s huge push into RCS.

That might finally be changing, though. Recent updates brought mention of RCS in the app’s code.

Now, a slightly newer version (v2026-11-01-1019342246) of Google Voice has debuted a redesign for the app on Android.

	

The new look isn’t a drastic restructuring, but a huge coat of paint on an app that hasn’t seen any meaningful updates since 2023. The new look feels more modern and very much influenced by Google Messages. The text field at the bottom has a rounded design with the same “+” and camera icons found in Messages, as well as a new long-press gesture that is, again, similar to Google’s primary messaging app. The main page hasn’t been updated beyond a new, rounded search bar up top and some subtly bolder fonts.

Material You colors are hit or miss now. On a Pixel with an orange theme, that color influenced the entire UI, but on a Galaxy Z Fold 8 with a coral/blue theme, the only sign of themeing was a blue message field. 

The most important thing here is the “SMS” icon on the send button, which looks just like the button in Google Messages. In that app, it’s used as an indicator as to what type of message you’re sending – SMS or RCS. Combined with code in that other recent update directly pointing to “RCS” being used on a send button, you can absolutely tell Google Voice is finally adding this long-overdue functionality.

A timeline for RCS support in Google Voice is still unclear, but this redesign going live now certainly suggests it’s coming sooner rather than later.

I can’t wait.

title: Google’s new ‘Fast Switch’ feature leaks, lets you use one number on two Android phones
snippet: Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool. more…
fullText:
Similar to a recent iPhone feature, Google appears to be working on “Fast Switch” as a way to share one SIM and phone number on two Android phones at once, and it sounds pretty cool.

Through the SIM Manager app on Android, the folks over at Android Authority noticed strings that tell a pretty clear story. 

A new feature called “Android Fast Switch” would let you “use your phone number on up to two phones,” with the SIM automatically switching to “whichever phone you unlock.” 

<string name=”companion_profile_title”>Use a SIM on two phones</string>

<string name=”companion_profile_description_prefix”>With Android Fast Switch, you can use your phone number on up to two phones. Mobile service automatically switches to whichever phone you unlock.</string>

<string name=”companion_profile_description_link”>Learn more about Android Fast Switch</string>

“Android Fast Switch” sounds nearly identical to Handoff on iPhone, a feature that lets iPhone owners share one SIM between two iPhones and quickly switch devices on the fly. 

	

Other strings explicitly say that you can “Use a SIM on two phones” and specify that both devices would need to be logged into the same Google account. One phone would be the “Primary” with the other as a “companion.”

There are still plenty of unknown details here, including what data might sync between devices as well as how carriers will respond. On iPhone, carriers either charge extra for this feature ($5 at T-Mobile, $10 at Verizon), or don’t support it at all (AT&T). We also don’t know what devices may be supported – this could easily end up as a Pixel-only affair.

	

As per usual with these early teardowns, though, the actual launch of a feature like this could be weeks, months, or even years away. Still, the idea itself is rather exciting. 

9to5Google’s Take

iPhone’s Handoff feature always sounded useful, but I personally always questioned why it would be useful on iPhone. With so little variety in hardware, the utility of switching between two iPhones seems somewhat dubious, outside of perhaps using a Mini or Air as a situational device alongside a Pro device.

On Android, the combinations are endless. It all just depends on what devices Google supports. What devices would you switch between?

fullText:
Each year, Apple Podcasts names its Show of the Year, and the 2026 winner is Baby, this is Keke Palmer. Apple said the podcast consistently ranked as one of the most popular shows, and praised it for its “exceptional quality and cultural impact” … 

For anyone unfamiliar, the show is an interview format, but aims to dig a little deeper than most.

Palmer invites some of the biggest names in entertainment and culture to share the experiences that have shaped them. From exploring self-worth with Oprah Winfrey to discussing creativity, reinvention, and fatherhood with Anderson .Paak, she moves effortlessly between laugh-out-loud exchanges and thoughtful reflections on life, relationships, and success […]

The show pairs Palmer’s quick wit with genuine curiosity, striking a balance between humor and thoughtful inquiry that makes even the most recognizable guests feel like close friends. Her natural ability to connect with people draws audiences into every conversation, while her candor and energy bring a refreshing and unique authenticity to the interview format.

Palmer said that authenticity was a key goal for the show, both for herself and for her guests, and she encourages other creators to take the same path.

Don’t try to manufacture a personality for the camera. Develop a relationship with yourself, get comfortable expressing what is already there, and let the camera capture that […]

Preparation is supposed to support the conversation, not control it. I’m always listening for that moment when somebody says something that opens up an entirely new question.

fullText:
Apple is working on its own AI agent that can perform a range of tasks for you, including browsing the web, working across apps, writing code, and calling services. That’s according to a now-removed job listing spotted by Bloomberg, which said Apple is looking for an engineer to lead the creation of an agentic AI assistant.

An AI agent from Apple would put the iPhone maker in the running to compete with the likes of Meta’s Muse, OpenAI’s Dots, Anthropic’s Duet, and Google’s Tasks. Muse, ChatGPT, and Perplexity can already take control of a computer through their Mac apps, while Google just started letting Gemini do the same.

Apple began rolling out its AI-upgraded Siri in September, which you can use to ask questions about what’s on your screen, as well as perform actions across apps. It looks like Apple is planning to give Siri more agentic capabilities, as a report from Bloomberg suggests the company could add the ability to rotate and crop images in Photos, or organize Safari tabs. This lines up with the company’s new job listing, which says the engineer will work closely with teams across its Siri, UI Frameworks, and Apple Foundation Models divisions.

“People already do their most valuable work by moving fluidly between tools: a browser, a document, a terminal, an editor, a service,” the job listing said. “We’re building AI agents that can do the same… These agents plan and carry out multi-step tasks across apps, browsers, command lines, code, and APIs, and they can coordinate specialized sub-agents along the way.”

With its upcoming iOS 27.3 update, Apple is also giving developers the ability to integrate Siri AI into “all apps.” This is rolling out as part of a Developer Preview and will eventually allow Siri to perform tasks across a wider range of apps.

Update, November 20th: Added that the job listing has since been removed.

title: The week everything fell apart
snippet: There was a dayslong Outlook outage. A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working. Even iCloud couldn't stay up and running. This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger. On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David go through the week's many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case - which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe - and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. In a world filled … Read the full story at The Verge.
fullText:
David Pierce

 

is editor-at-large and Vergecast co-host with over a decade of experience covering consumer tech. Previously, at Protocol, The Wall Street Journal, and Wired.

There was a dayslong Outlook outage. A nationwide ground stop for only the second time in 25 years. Banks seemed to suddenly stop working. Even iCloud couldn’t stay up and running. This week, it felt like the technological world simply collapsed. And it felt like this might be the beginning of something even bigger.

On this episode of The Vergecast, Nilay and David go through the week’s many calamities, and try to explain both what happened in each case — which was generally much milder than the conspiracy theories would have you believe — and why all these small issues might still add up to something worth worrying about. In a world filled with more AI and fewer humans, we’re going to see new kinds of problems and often struggle to find the fixes.

After that, the hosts discuss the latest in the Jensen Huang / Nvidia scandal, which is increasingly less about affairs and more about the allegedly very big business of illegally smuggling chips to China. Huang will not be back as Nvidia CEO anytime soon, no matter what a bunch of X users want, and the fallout of his exit seems likely to only increase.

Finally, in the lightning round, it’s time for Brendan Carr is a Dummy, Nilay’s experience with his always-listening Apple Watch, Google’s inability to name products, and much more.

In case you missed it this week: We also talked about e-readers, computer chips, GTA VI, and the world after GTA VI. And we want to hear all your thoughts about all of it! snippet: Motorola’s Moto Tag 2 is the only Find Hub tracker for Android with UWB support besides the new Google Pixel Tag, and the former is currently at its lowest price ever for Black Friday at just $19. more…
fullText:
Motorola’s Moto Tag 2 is the only Find Hub tracker for Android with UWB support besides the new Google Pixel Tag, and the former is currently at its lowest price ever for Black Friday at just $19.

Nearly half off its retail price, Moto Tag 2 is currently just $18.99 on Amazon for Black Friday. The Moto Tag 2 may not be quite as deeply integrated into Google’s Find Hub as the Pixel Tag is, but it has all of the same core features. It also comes with the advantage of having a design that works alongside Apple’s AirTag accessories.

If I were looking to stock up this Black Friday, I’d be picking Moto Tag 2 over the Pixel Tag at these prices. Even in a 4-pack, Pixel Tag is much more expensive, and Moto Tag 2 works great. Plus, Pixel Tag shipments (at least from Amazon) are delayed right now anyway.

title: Google Pixel Tag is coming to Europe ‘pretty soon,’ leak says
snippet: The Pixel Tag will begin selling in Europe soon, according to a recent leak. The Android Find Hub tracker sold nearly everywhere else during the initial launch. more…
fullText:
The Pixel Tag will begin selling in Europe soon, according to a recent leak. The Android Find Hub tracker sold nearly everywhere else during the initial launch.

Google’s very first tracker joined the dozens of other options that work on the Android Find Hub network, launching alongside the Pixel 11 earlier in the year. It’s a sleek little tracking tag, with some first-party care that makes it stand out.

Leaker Roland Quandt posted an update on the Pixel Tag in a recent Bluesky post. It states the Pixel Tag will, in fact, be sold in Europe. There’s no timeline indication in the post, other than a wide-open “pretty soon” tagged on at the end.

 It’s a wonder it didn’t launch in Europe to begin with. Google initially listed 8 countries, including the US, Canada, Australia, India, and Japan. The United Kingdom is included in that list, but the larger portion classified as the European Union is left out.

	

The leak also eases a major concern for users – whether the Pixel Tag will be operational in Europe at all. The Pixel Tag would likely function among the network of Android users in the varying regions, but there’s no definitive answer. But if the Pixel Tag officially lands in Europe, then users won’t need to worry about whether network support will be available.

The Pixel Tag is currently available for nearly every other region online.
